speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: SOUTH AFRICA
subsubtopic: MESSAGE OF CONDOLENCE ON DEATH OF PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I know that hon. members would wish to associate themselves with a message of condolence which I sent to his colleagues on learning of the death yesterday of the Prime Minister of South Africa, Hon. Johannes Gerhardus Strijdom.
Mr. Strijdom long struggled against serious illness, and until a short time ago continued against odds the service he had so long given to his country. Born in 1893 in what was then Cape Colony, Mr. Strijdom became a farmer, a civil servant, a lawyer and a journalist. Throughout his life he continued to be interested in agriculture and journalism. In 1929 he was elected a member of parliament for Waterberg in the Transvaal, a seat he continued to hold. In 1934 he became joint leader of the National party in the Transvaal. When in 1948 the National party took office he was appointed minister of lands and irrigation, and in 1954 succeeded Dr. Malan as prime minister and leader in chief of the National party.
In an active political career lasting through a generation, Mr. Strijdom spared no effort in the public service of his country. I am sure I speak for the house in extending the sympathy of Canada to his widow, the government, and the people of South Africa.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: COMMUNIST CHINA
speechtext:
As hon. members are well aware, there have been disturbing reports of increased communist Chinese activity
against the nationalist-held islands in Taiwan straits. Since the cessation of the attacks of 1955 it had been hoped that the Peking regime, while disputing jurisdiction over these islands, would not again threaten the peace in this area. At this time I have in mind the concern which I am sure all of us share regarding the grave consequences which may ensue if the Chinese communists resort to force to settle issues in the Taiwan straits.
The United States has a mutual defence treaty with the nationalist Chinese government, and it would of course be for the United States government to decide the nature of its obligations in case of an attempt by the communist Chinese government to alter the status quo in the coastal islands of Formosa strait or of Formosa itself.
I take this occasion to assure the house that the Canadian government has no commitment to involve itself in a dispute over this territory between the two Chinese authorities.

subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE

speakeroldname: Hon. G. R. Pearkes (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF UNIFICATION OF MEDICAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure hon. members will be interested to hear that a decision has been reached to combine the medical services of the navy, army and air force into one unified medical service. This decision has been taken after careful study extending over many months, and is in line with the recommendations of the estimates committee.
The unification will commence on the 1st of January, 1959, and it is intended to include in the plan all medical officers, nursing sisters and non-medical administrative officers. Planning to this end is now proceeding at national defence headquarters, care being taken that the interest of all three armed forces is protected.
The new armed forces medical service will be placed under the direction of a surgeon general, who will be assisted by a single medical headquarters in Ottawa in place of four such medical headquarters as previously existed. Similarly, there will be subordinate regional medical headquarters appropriately located in relation to armed forces requirements both in Canada and abroad. The total number of regional headquarters will be, as a result of their unified character, considerably less than has been the case in the past.

Motion for Papers
In reaching this decision I have had the advice of the Canadian armed forces medical council, which body includes prominent members of the civilian medical profession. I am satisfied that this move will result in more efficient and economical provision of medical services for the armed forces. As a result of unification, the professional development and career prospects of medical officers will be greatly improved.

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-55, to establish a board of broadcast governors and to provide for the continuance of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in rising to move the second reading of this bill, which is of great importance, I could perhaps be forgiven if I spoke at considerable length. Certainly the subject matter warrants it. But in view of the fact that I have already spoken

on three previous occasions this session on the matter of broadcasting generally, 1 am sure the house will understand-and will even appreciate it-if I speak very briefly on this occasion.
There are one or two preliminary remarks I should like to make before referring to the bill itself. The Leader of the Opposition, in speaking on the resolution the other night, as did the hon. member for Bonavista-Twil-lingate and, I think, other hon. members, suggested that the bill be introduced and allowed to stand until another session. The government cannot accept that suggestion, and proposes to go forward with this legislation, in the hope that it will meet with the approval of the parliament of Canada, and to enact it in due course.
There are various reasons for this. One, I think, is very obvious. It was in 1955 that a royal commission was appointed to consider broadcasting in Canada, and there had been much discussion prior to that date regarding the attitude which the government of that day would take toward broadcasting. Therefore, from at least 1955 down to the present time there has been an atmosphere of uncertainty with respect to broadcasting generally and in particular with reference to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, and I do not think it would be fair to the staff of that organization, the people who are heading it and the thousands who are engaged in it to continue this atmosphere any longer.
I think Canada owes a great debt to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, its officials and its personnel, for the work they have done, and it is certainly a tribute to their morale that they have been able to carry on as they have during these uncertain days. For that reason, if for no others, I think it will commend itself to the house that the bill be enacted and the situation clarified so that both the C.B.C. and the private stations may know what is ahead of them and what will be done. We therefore propose to proceed with this legislation in due course.
One other remark should be made at this time. At the opening of parliament this government undertook to have a committee appointed to deal with this legislation. That was an undertaking given on behalf of the government and, of course, we are prepared to carry it out. If the house requests it a committee will be appointed after the bill has received second reading, and the measure will go to that committee. The spokesmen for the C.C.F. group indicated the other day that the opinion of their group was that it was not advisable to have a committee at this time. As I say, with regard to that matter the government is in the hands of the
57071-3-256
Broadcasting
house, but I would point out that the legislation creates a framework and nothing else; it establishes a board of broadcast governors; it reconstitutes and reaffirms the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, and lays down certain broad general principles. The details have to be filled in by regulation and, frankly, I do not know just what a committee could do at this stage in dealing with this bill.
If there were obvious objections to the bill in principle and there was a possibility of having those objections at least aired, if not corrected, in committee, I could understand why the bill should go there. But I think on the whole, if I may be forgiven for saying so, this bill has met with general acceptance across the country. We can see that from the editorials and the general comment in the press. If the bill were to go to a committee today or tomorrow, just what could be done about the details? We could not ask about the regulations, because the regulations are going to be prepared by a body which has not yet been constituted; and if we were asked as to the personnel, I can say this quite frankly. This government has given no consideration whatsoever to the appointment of the personnel of the board of broadcast governors and/or the board of directors of the C.B.C. We have been dealing with broad general principles, and we have not given consideration to the personnel thus if a committee were constituted and were to ask who was going to be on the board, I should have to say frankly that we had no idea at all.
I have received several hundred letters, I may say, from persons suggesting that they have all the qualifications necessary for such appointments, and I have received as many letters from people suggesting names which they consider to be highly suitable.

speechtext:
Broadcasting
which hon. gentlemen know always accumulate during a session. Then it will give consideration to the personnel of these two boards.
When they will be appointed I cannot say, but knowing something of how governments work and the time it takes with respect to a broad national board to select personnel representative of this whole country, taking into consideration its vast geographic areas and all the rest of it, it is obvious the board is not going to be appointed too soon after parliament rises. I would think, as a matter of fact, the board would just nicely be in operation and have begun drafting regulations and so on when this parliament again reconvenes.
On behalf of the government, Mr. Speaker, I would say that if it is requested at the next session of parliament, we will shortly after the session begins set up a special committee of the house to deal with radio and broadcasting generally. All these matters can be referred to that committee, and perhaps the committee can watch the organization take shape and form and grow during the session rather than speculate, which is all we can do now concerning the operation of the bill.
As to the bill itself, there are two broad general principles laid down. The Prime Minister before the election, as did other hon. members of this party in years gone by, stated that he felt it was inadvisable to have the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation acting in a dual capacity in, both passing and operating regulations and passing judgment on broadcasting. One of the fundamental principles this government wanted to see was the divorcing of those two functions, the operating and the regulatory. This bill does that. Through the medium of this bill we will have established the legislative framework for a broad national board of 15 members, three full time and the others part time, who will be entrusted with the various duties laid down by this bill. The principle set forth in clause 10 of the bill is, I think, worthy of repeating here:
The board shall, for the purpose of ensuring the continued existence and efficient operation of a national broadcasting system and the provision of a varied and comprehensive broadcasting service of a high standard that is basically Canadian in content and character, regulate the establishment and operation of networks of broadcasting stations, the activities of public and private broadcasting stations in Canada and the relationship between them and provide for the final determination of all matters and questions in relation thereto.
That, Mr. Speaker, is the crux of the situation. You cannot legislate good broadcasting; that is impossible. You can have the best act in the world, and if the right personnel are not appointed to these boards then the act
[Mr. Nowlan.l
will be a failure. On the other hand you can have a poor act and obtain the very best results because of the personnel who are selected. As I see it, Mr. Speaker, that is the core of this matter.
Incidentally, as a side note, I wish to relate an incident that occurred the other day. I was speaking to a former member of the original board governing broadcasting who told me that when the broadcasting bill was brought down by the Bennett government, I think in 1932, the government had spent weeks and months drafting the bill. It was discussed in parliament at great length and went through a committee where it was carefully examined. Everything was done in connection with the bill. Before the board held its first meeting it was found that the bill contained one clause which made it practically inoperative. Despite that flaw in the legislation they carried on with their work.
That is one thing that is established by the present bill, the board of broadcast governors, which will have general supervision over private and public broadcasting in Canada. I wish to pay my tribute here to those involved in the C.B.C. and public broadcasting generally, and to the private broadcasters as well. There are varying records of performance in those groups, but on the whole a great deal has been done and this country has been extremely fortunate in its public and private broadcasting and the co-operation that has existed between private broadcasters and the C.B.C. I am sure this co-operation will continue in the future.
It will be the policy of this government in selecting personnel to select no one who is associated with broadcasting in any way. There may be obvious defects in that policy, but there are also obvious advantages. Also, no one who is not a Canadian citizen can be selected. The thought is that this board, wisely chosen as I trust and believe it will be, will develop, strengthen and maintain broadcasting in Canada in an integrated system, both public and private.
The other phase of this bill, of course, concerns the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, which is continued. The name "board of governors" has been dropped for obvious reasons. We will now have a board of broadcast governors and the name "director" has been chosen in its place. This corporation will be continued and will have the operative-and only the operative-factors of the broadcasting system under its responsibility and control.
Those, Mr. Speaker, are the broad general outlines of this bill, coupled with the fact that to the board shall be given the power to make regulations on a broad basis; and

on those regulations and their enforcement will depend the success or failure of the future of broadcasting in this country.
I will not anticipate the debate, but I know there are certain comments which could be made to which I will probably have the opportunity of replying. It is not for me to express the hope as to when the bill will be passed, but I believe I have said sufficient for the time being to sketch the broad outlines of this bill, and I commend it to this house for its favourable consideration.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of ihe Opposition):
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister and I hope the house will forgive me if I spend a great deal more time on the second reading of this bill than the minister did at this stage in the debate. The minister will also perhaps not be surprised if I do not share the satisfaction he has expressed about this bill, or if I attribute a great deal more importance to it than he has indicated in his remarks that he attaches to it at the present time.
The minister said the bill was more or less in the nature of a framework which would have to be filled in by administration and operation. I believe it is much more than that, and I shall endeavour to indicate as I go along why I take that view. As a matter of fact, it is because we consider this bill so important and indeed so complicated that we condemn the government for introducing it along with two other bills of major importance, one on customs procedures and one on human rights, in the dying days of a long and exhausting session. We consider that this procedure in regard to a bill of this importance is indefensible.
The minister said that if we requested a parliamentary committee to be set up this session the government would accept that suggestion, because it saw fit to include such a reference in the speech from the throne. But the minister also indicated, and it is a hope shared by a great many people, that this session will be brought to an end within a short period of time. If that is the case, much as we would like to see a committee deal with this bill in this session, there certainly would be no opportunity at this time for such a committee to give the kind of consideration to this bill which is required. The committee should have an opportunity of calling witnesses and receiving submissions and views of interested parties affected by this bill. There would be, I fear, through a committee set up this session no opportunity now of giving this bill the careful, complete and unhurried committee examination which its importance certainly warrants.
On behalf of the government the minister has rejected the other suggestion I ventured 57071-3-256J
Broadcasting
to make when we were discussing the resolution before the introduction of this bill, namely that it should be held over until the next session when it could be considered as a bill, not as an act, by a committee of the house which would be set up at that time. The reason the minister seems to object to this is that it would leave the whole situation in an uncertain position; that it would prolong the uncertainty which now exists in regard to broadcasting in this country, and that it is desirable to get this matter cleared up at once by the passage of this bill. But the minister also said, and I think he was right in saying it, that it is going to take quite a long time to appoint all the members of those two boards. If I heard him correctly, he indicated it might take almost the whole of the intervening period between now and the calling of the next session to make the appointments.
If that is true, and it may well be true because, as the minister says, it takes a lot of time to make appointments of this kind- and there are 25 to be made under this bill -then that uncertainty which he talked about will be prolonged, whether we pass this bill or not, until even the next session. Therefore that argument, it seems to me, against submitting this bill to a committee next session for the kind of consideration which it should get, falls to the ground.
Apparently the government has decided to rush this bill through at the end, or just before the end, of this session. That procedure is to be condemned all the more because we on this side brought the necessity of an early declaration of legislative policy on this matter to the attention of the government six weeks ago; I think it was six weeks ago today. Well, apparently this procedure which we suggested as the most sensible, the most democratic form of procedure to take, of submitting this bill to a committee at the next session of parliament after it has been given preliminary consideration at this session, is not to be adopted. We regret that, because it seems to us a procedure which would respect both the rights and the responsibilities of parliament and of the public. Even now, in spite of what the minister has said, I plead with the government to reconsider the matter and perhaps adopt this course.
I rest my case for that plea on the fact that this is an important and complicated bill, indeed a bill of the highest importance in the national development of this country. It is not a bill which is easy to understand in all its details. However, we are now on second reading, and I assure the minister that we on this side will do our best to bring

Broadcasting
the weaknesses ol this bill to the attention of the government. We shall give it the detailed consideration, in so far as we are able, which it deserves when it reaches the committee stage. Certainly, as I have just said, its importance in our view can hardly be exaggerated.
In no sector of our national life more than in the field of broadcasting is there a greater and more continuing need for strong and independent public service and public control. This sentiment has been expressed more than once in this house, and by the minister himself, that to strengthen and preserve our cultural life and ultimately perhaps develop and preserve our national identity, broadcasting should be brought and maintained under strong public control. Canadian ownership and control of our material heritage, of our natural resources, of our means of production is, of course, as necessary as it is desirable; but that control would lose a great deal of its significance in our continued development as a nation if we lost public control over this important aspect of our non-material life, of our cultural life.
This was certainly appreciated in the earliest days of parliamentary consideration of broadcasting legislation, Mr. Speaker. Certainly earlier statutes-I propose to mention two of them-were not rushed through parliament. I go back to 1932, when the first basic broadcasting legislation in this country was introduced by Right Hon. R. B. Bennett in a bill in that year. Before that bill was introduced-and I commend this precedent to my hon. friend-the Aird royal commission had been discussing broadcasting for many, many months, I think perhaps for as long a period of time, though I may not be accurate in this, as the Fowler commission. Indeed, the Aird commission was set up, I think, in 1929 and Mr. Bennett brought in his bill in 1932.
But in spite of the consideration given to the matter by that commission a parliamentary committee was set up at once, consisting of nine members of the House of Commons. That committee gave very careful and non-partisan consideration to the report of the Aird commission. The committee met 26 times over a period of six weeks and received 53 briefs and submissions. It then made a unanimous report to the house. It was on the report of that parliamentary committee that the 1932 legislation was based.
Again, in 1936 new broadcasting legislation-there had been some amendments to the earlier act before this-was brought in by the Liberal government. Again a parliamentary committee was set up before that legislation was considered in this house,

consisting of 23 members who met for two months and gave very careful study to the whole matter. Twenty-five meetings were held and 37 witnesses were heard. That report, as hon. members will recall, recommended the repeal of the 1932 act and the setting up of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation as it has existed since that time.
In those days, Mr. Speaker, we had careful, exhaustive parliamentary examination before legislation was passed. That procedure reflected the concern about public and parliamentary control of this vital national service, concern which was felt not only by members of parliament but by the people of Canada, and concern which they still feel today, concern over the necessity of doing nothing by legislation to interfere with a strong and independent national broadcasting system.
At the first stage of public and parliamentary consideration of this matter, the first stage of Canadian radio history was that perhaps initiated by the Aird report in which, remember, it was proposed to establish a public broadcasting agency in Canada which would take over and absorb all the private stations operating at that time. It was felt that broadcasting should be exclusively a public service.
The second stage began with the act of 1932, when it was decided to have a single national broadcasting system which would be operated basically as a public service; but private stations would be permitted to function, I emphasize, under the control and regulation of the public agency as an integrated part of a national system to complement on a local and regional basis the public element which was to remain in any case the heart and backbone of the national system.
When private stations were given this complementary and important role at that time under the direct supervision of the public broadcasting agency, that meant that we did have indeed a single national broadcasting system operating primarily as a public service. Experience since that time has shown that the private stations, under the conditions I have mentioned, could and did render very useful services and in a manner very profitable to themselves.
We must bear in mind, however, that an essential and clearly recognizable feature of that system was that these private stations had no special rights of their own. They had a privilege granted to them by the government, and it was a profitable one, of being part of a national system. In a sense they had, rights of course, but only rights as part of that national system. If they were granted more rights it was feared that the national

system might suffer, that pressures on government might develop which would be too strong for the independence of the public element of the national system.
The minister may remepiber that the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett was one who warned against that possibility in the 1930's. It is interesting to note that he argued strenuously against the 1936 bill because he thought that placing the licensing authority under the Department of Transport would put the C.B.C. "completely under the power of the government and expose it to pressures and influences which would weaken its national character." Mr. Bennett was particularly worried that the government would not be able to withstand pressures from private broadcasters who, he warned the Commons of that day, as found on page 3710 of Hansard, tor June 15, 1936, "have been watchful of their own interests and have determined that if it is within their power this facility"-radio broadcasting-"is not to function as a public enterprise."
These direct pressures may have been resisted and I think were resisted more effectively than Mr. Bennett thought would happen but, of course, they have not ceased, and none of us needs to be surprised at this. The fact that they have not ceased was shown by the presentation of a brief to the Fowler commission by the Canadian association of radio and television broadcasters, Exhibit 312, in which they proposed that in principle the burden of providing broadcasting facilities to the nation should be largely shifted from the shoulders of the Canadian taxpayers to Canadian industry. The implication of that statement is clear and it arouses all the more anxiety in us because over the years we have perhaps begun to lose sight of the initially accepted doctrine of public control through a national system and of the vital necessity of maintaining and strengthening that system.
What was at once, for instance, as I have stated, a privilege for private broadcasters has gradually become a vested interest and eventually has been invoked as a right. As soon as this privilege could be put forward in public discussion as a right, which of course it was not, then the position of the C.B.C., the public corporation, could be attacked on the ground that the public agency was at the same time a judge and a competitor. Under our system of broadcasting over the years since 1936 the C.B.C. in one sense, and perhaps it was an undesirable sense, was a judge controlling, appraising and supervising certain aspects of the operations of private stations. But that was always done within the framework of the essential features of our national system. Strictly speaking the C.B.C. was not a competitor with the private stations, as those
Broadcasting
stations did not have separate rights to claim but rights which were merely an extension and complement of the national system.
I have dwelt on this matter at some length because it seems to me it is quite important for us to bear in mind the historical background and these essential features of our present broadcasting system as we consider the proposed legislation which, it may be argued, makes only superficial framework changes in our set-up, changes designed merely to eliminate-and I am not objecting to this-the so-called incompatibility of functions of the C.B.C., and to assure just and fair treatment to the private stations. While the bill may appear to be doing only that, if it is studied carefully and analysed in all its possible implications I suggest it may be found to change in a substantial way the very basis of our broadcasting system. Perhaps it would be more accurate to say that it is a sanctioning by law of changes which had been creeping in.
Members of the house and the Canadian public should be very clear as to what the government is proposing to do in the bill, because once a decision has been made with regard to it, it will be very difficult indeed to reverse any undesirable consequences of that decision and change again the broadcasting set-up we are now being asked to approve. On second reading, of course, the criticisms I propose to put forward will be general in character, because we will have an opportunity in committee to deal with the specific clauses of the bill.
As I see it, however, there are certain major defects in the legislation. First, in my view it goes a long way toward creating two national broadcasting systems. Second, it weakens the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in some undesirable ways. Third, it provides for an undesirable and cumbersome administrative setup. There are, of course, some good features in the bill, but it is not my purpose to dwell on them. I thought the minister would have spent a little time on the good features of the bill when he spoke.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext: How are you going to vote on it?

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext:
I will come to that. If my hon. friend has any doubt on that matter that doubt will very soon be clearly removed. There are, of course, some good features in the bill which may improve the national system, and by facilitating the extension of that system in its private and public elements may give viewers more and varied television and radio enjoyment. This will depend, as the minister has pointed out in other contexts, on how it is set up and administered. If that can be done through private as well as public

Broadcasting
stations without weakening the national system as a whole, that will be fine. The viewer and the listener are certainly entitled to every reasonable and practicable consideration in this matter.
On the other hand, and it is the other hand about which I am concerned at the moment, there are provisions in this bill which I consider to be harmful and perhaps retrogressive. This might not worry us so much if the provisions of this bill when it becomes law were to be implemented and enforced by a government composed of persons who in the past had shown that they really believed in a strong, independent Canadian broadcasting corporation as the mainspring, the essential part, of our national system, and who could be counted upon to use the provisions of this bill for that purpose. However, the opinions of some of the members of the government as recorded in Hansard do not give us too much confidence in that regard.
My first criticism then, Mr. Speaker, and I am going to dwell on this at some length because I think it is a very important criticism, is that this bill might weaken the principle of one national system. We have been told by the minister on more than one occasion that this bill is based on the recommendations of the Fowler commission. This commission, in its report, warns us more than once against any action which might lead to the creation of two systems of broadcasting in this country, one public and one private. It is my submission that this bill could lead to just that.
I know, of course, that section 10 of the bill, to which I think the minister referred a few minutes ago, mentions the continued existence and efficient operation of the national broadcasting system as an aim and objective of the new regulatory body. But in fact, as I see it this bill, whether intentionally or not, may have the opposite effect. Under it the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation complies with regulations imposed by the proposed board of broadcast governors, and will conduct its activities separately. It will have its own responsible minister through whom it will report to parliament, and not through the board of broadcast governors.
On their part the private stations, whether they operate separately or as a part of a network, will be now entirely apart from the C.B.C. Certainly this bill, as I interpret it, gives the C.B.C. no special position, no predominance which would enable it to discharge more effectively its national responsibility. Both the private and public sectors of broadcasting would, as I read the bill, appear as equals before the new board which

would regulate their separate activities and their relationship. This board would report to parliament through its minister independently of the C.B.C. board. There are some who may approve of this, but I am not one of them because I feel that this provision may well lead for all practical purposes to the serious weakening, with all the consequences that may follow from that weakening, of the single national system, something we have always considered to be essential and which indeed is put forward as a main objective of the bill itself.
This seems to me a very important change from the concept of broadcasting in Canada which we have held in the past. First, as I have said, the private stations were to disappear. Then it was realized, and quite rightly, that they could be of value on the local and regional level. It was decided therefore, as I tried to point out, that they should operate in that way, complementing the public service. Now under this legislation the private stations would secure equal rights with the C.B.C. before the new board.
While it may appear that the two elements in the system, private and public, have equal rights before this new board of broadcast governors, in fact it is clear that their position before that board will not be the same. The private broadcasters, while rendering a valuable service-and we on this side have always admitted the value of that service-have to make a profit to survive. They must continually keep that necessity in mind when they appear before the new board. Such things as more advertising, lower costs through minimum regulations and standards, the Canadian content of programs, and so on, would naturally be their main preoccupation when they appear before this new board.
I know, and the Fowler commission confirms it, that the C.B.C. did not always exercise adequate control over private stations in their programming. I ask, will the new board do better, especially in the face of the new and more independent status achieved by the private stations? Will the new board not have as a major consideration the financial problems and costs in determining the program standards and advertising control? Its regulations, however, cannot discriminate between public and private stations. These regulations will have to be the same for everybody, and as a result it may well be that the uniform standards which will have to be adopted by the new board will have to fit the financial situation of the weakest private station, even if it is part of a C.B.C. network and is subsidized in the same way as now happens by the C.B.C. Will there not be a danger that the standards

which will be laid down as of uniform application will be too low? I suggest that this is a danger, even though in practice those standards applied by the C.B.C. will be, as I certainly hope they will be, higher than those prescribed by the board for all stations.
In short, Mr. Speaker, what I am trying to point out is the danger that under this legislation broadcasting in Canada may cease to be conducted by a single national system, mainly as a public service, and we may come to have two systems, one public and one private, becoming more and more independent of each other and having equal rights and status. They will tend then to develop along parallel lines, meeting before the new board only when operating licences are discussed or disputes decided. Therefore, instead of clarifying and strengthening the present situation this bill is likely to create confusion and uncertainty. It certainly raises many doubts and some anxieties.
This new board of broadcast governors, because the C.B.C. program standards will likely be above the minimum prescribed, will tend to become a regulatory body for private stations only, influenced increasingly by the financial situation of those private stations. More and more, then, this board may be concerned with private stations rather than the control and regulation of a national system. I submit, Mr. Speaker, there is a very real danger in this to that system. Surely in the light of this possibility, and it is a real possibility, this bill with all it involves and with all it implies should have been reserved for the most careful and critical examination of a parliamentary committee before it was either adopted or rejected.
Another basic weakness of this new bill which bears on the dangers to the national system which I have mentioned is that it provides for two boards of a generally comparable character. If these two boards do not get into each other's way, or indeed into each other's hair, with resulting confusion and conflict it will be because one of them-more likely perhaps the C.B.C. board-will become more or less useless. The Fowler commission report has been put forward as the basis of the legislation which the government should adopt, but let us see what that report had to say on this very important point of two boards. I read from page 134 of the report:
But suppose . . . we had the two boards set up today;
And that is what is being proposed.
-one, a board to supervise the operations of C.B.C., the other a board to regulate and control the operations of both C.B.C. and private stations and to deal with licensing matters.
Broadcasting
The report goes on:
The two boards, composed of people of similar background and qualifications, operating in many of the same fields and necessarily in close contact with each other either would draw together or pull apart. If all were harmonious between them, if they generally thought alike and agreed with each other, the situation would quickly become indistinguishable from that existing today; except that it would be more cumbersome to have a double review of many issues and more expensive to the taxpayer. Alternatively, if the two bodies (as is probably more likely) pulled apart, one or other would be bound to assert dominance, through the skill and strength of personality of its members, especially of its chairman. If the C.B.C. board became dominant, the regulatory body would tend to become a cipher; it would be an extra expense and formality to approve, generally, what the C.B.C. wanted. On the other hand, if the regulatory board became dominant, and the real centre of power, the C.B.C. board would become unimportant, and real control would be exercised by the regulatory body over both the C.B.C. and the private stations as well. As far as management of C.B.C. was concerned it would be frustrated; as far as control was concerned it would probably become a more active and onerous regulation of private stations by the body interested in and dominating the C.B.C.-the very basis of the present complaint.
This excerpt from the report concludes:
As a practical matter, we do not believe you can have two administrative bodies, appointed by the same government and with similar personnel involved in the regulation of broadcasting, without having duplication of expense and effort, undesirable friction between the two, and a loss of efficiency.
This leads me to our second criticism of this bill, which is indeed implicit in what I have been saying; namely that this bill might lead to the weakening of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I have already implied that this might happen and if it does happen it will be very unfortunate indeed. But having said that, I would like to make it perfectly clear that if we on this side of the house are opposed-as we are opposed-to any measure which in our view tends to reduce the independence and efficiency of the C.B.C., we would also be opposed to anything which would result in unfair treatment of the private sector of broadcasting.
I cheerfully admit that there are some provisions in this bill which from the point of view of the private broadcasters might perhaps give them fairer treatment in some matters. We have always said and we still believe that the private broadcasters up to today have rendered a very useful service to Canada. In certain instances they could no doubt have improved their standards, as pointed out by the Fowler commission, but we on this side of the house believe that in spite of some deficiencies-and the C.B.C. has also shown evidence of some deficiencies-the private broadcasters now constitute an integral and valuable part of our national system.

Broadcasting
Having said this I wish to emphasize once again, because I think it requires repeated emphasis, that we in this party still believe that broadcasting in Canada should remain, in the interests of national development if for no other reason, basically a public service. Furthermore we believe that the expansion and the independence of the C.B.C. as an agency indispensable to our national system should continue to be preserved, guaranteed and strengthened. We do not find any satisfactory guarantee in that respect in this proposed bill. On the contrary we believe that the status of the C.B.C. is weakened by it in several ways, and whether or not one approves of that weakening, I think it is important to know the facts of the matter.
In the first place this bill does not give the C.B.C. clear control of its own networks. That control, as I read it, is not clearly assured in this bill. In the second place, in this bill- and perhaps there are those who would approve of this-the C.B.C. loses its power to recommend the issuance of new licences, which power is transferred to the new board of broadcasting governors. This could prevent the C.B.C. from expanding when it is required, and could interfere with its competitive position vs-a-vis the private broadcasters.
Whether this will happen will largely depend, of course, on the personnel of that board, and I fully agree with the minister that this is a vitally important feature of this legislation. The minister said the other night that any piece of legislation in the world can operate only as well as those who are appointed to administer it, and perhaps no legislation which has come before this house for a long time has made this fact more apparent and indeed obvious; because in this legislation 25 men are to be appointed to administer it. Nevertheless, while it is true that so much does depend upon the administration and upon the calibre of the men appointed for that purpose, the possibility I have mentioned with respect to the weakening of the C.B.C. is, in my opinion, more likely to be realized under this bill if the new board operates in some of the ways I have mentioned. If the minister when he replies could assure me on this point I would be most grateful.
A third danger to the C.B.C. as a result of this bill is, as I see it, that the new administrative set-up of the corporation will become more cumbersome, and its independence will be somewhat less than that which now exists. It will have its own board, but its activities will be subject also to regulation, at least in principle, by the new board of broadcast governors. It will also have to submit its activities for approval to the responsible minister each year-also to the 
Minister of Finance, and I will come back to that in a moment,-and to the governor in council and finally to parliament. It will readily be seen that in this procedure there will be opportunities to restrict the C.B.C.'s activities, to discourage leadership and enterprise within the C.B.C., and to tamper with its independence which is so essential to the corporation.
I would like to support that statement by reference to some of the provisions of the bill in question. The C.B.C. will now not only be shorn of its former power and influence in the maintenance and development of the national system but will, I think, now be more exposed than it has been to the possibility of political interference. It was this operating phase of the C.B.C. that the Fowler commission wanted to protect against the ever-present threat of government interference, and that was one of the primary reasons why the commission recommended a single board of governors.
I suggest that the bill before us does not safeguard the C.B.C. sufficiently against this danger. Under existing legislation the operating personnel of the C.B.C. from the general manager down are insulated, if I may use that word, from direct political pressure and political interference by the presence of a board of governors and a full time chairman of that board. That particular form of insulation has now been removed.
Perhaps the minister will say that something else has been put in its place, but I suggest that the new insulation is not going to be as effective as the old. The senior executive of the corporation now will be the president, who will also function as chairman of the board of governors of the corporation, which means that the responsible minister will now deal directly with the senior operating officer of the corporation-the president-instead of with an officer removed from day to day operation, the chairman. The new board will no longer be able to act, as it did formerly, as a protective shield for those concerned with the development, production and broadcasting of programs.
I am coming to the end of my criticisms, the minister will be glad to learn. However, there is a fourth and, I think, very important consideration, and one which makes us critical of this bill. It has a bearing on this matter of political interference which I have just mentioned, and it concerns the financial provisions of the bill which, we think, are such as to weaken rather than strengthen the independence of the C.B.C. from government. At the present time, as the minister knows, parliament has earmarked specific sources of revenue to the C.B.C. which, together with

the income derived from commercial operations, ensures at least a degree of financial independence. During some years it allowed a very high degree of financial independence, though I agree that in recent years the gap between those revenues and the needs of the C.B.C., especially in the field of television, has been increasing and has had to be filled by annual appropriations by parliament.
As the minister knows, the Fowler commission devoted a great deal of time to this financial problem. In fact that was the main reason why this commission was set up in the first place. And the conclusion of the Fowler commission which, I think, is rejected in this bill, was that a very high degree of financial independence had to be maintained in order to prevent unwarranted governmental interference with operations and to permit sound planning. The commission put forward what were, in its consideration, three possible methods of financing designed to preserve the prerogatives of parliament, to maintain the independence of the C.B.C. and to meet the need of the corporation for funds, a need which was bound to grow in the years ahead. In that connection the commission said on page 256:
The greatest financial weakness of the C.B.C. has been the lack of an assured and definite basis of current financing.
I do not intend at this stage to discuss the merits of the various suggestions which were put forward by the Fowler commission or, indeed, of other suggestions which have been put forward to ensure that the weakness referred to by the commission might be removed. At the present moment, during this debate on second reading, I am more interested in the very important principle which is involved here of establishing, in so far as it can be established, the reasonable financial independence of the corporation so it can plan ahead. I am quite confident that a practical solution safeguarding this principle, and also safeguarding the principle of parliamentary control, could be found if the government desired to find one, but it seems to me that the present bill neglects both these principles and the recommendations of the Fowler report concerning them. This is one of the things that worry us most about this legislation, and it is one of the reasons we do not find it acceptable.
If the proposed legislation is approved the C.B.C. will have no independent source of revenue whatever except the revenue it derives from its commercial operations. Not the listener, nor the viewer, but the taxpayer will pay everything else, and its financing will therefore depend to a much greater degree 57071-3-257
Broadcasting
than formerly on the discretion of the Minister of Finance, whose views on the C.B.C. are well known, and on the minister responsible, and on the governor in council.
That, as I have said, is one of the disturbing features of this legislation which we cannot accept. We fear that using this system of annual appropriations and nothing else under a government not too enthusiastic about the C.B.C.-and we have no reason to believe the present government is too enthusiastic about it-the activities and the necessary expansion of the corporation could be prejudiced and the power of the purse used annually could impose the views of government in a field where this kind of interference could be damaging to the right of the people to be informed objectively.
I am not stating, Mr. Speaker, that this will happen, but I do state that it could more easily happen under this legislation than it could under the previous legislation.
This proposed method of financing also hampers the management with regard to planning its operations ahead over a reasonable period of time. I agree that in the bill before us, clause 35, subclause 2, the corporation is required every five years to submit to the minister to whom it is responsible, and to the Minister of Finance, a capital expenditure program covering a five-year period, but there is nothing in this provision which stipulates that this program must be submitted to parliament for consideration, or even made public. If a government chose, that report could become merely an accounting exercise.
It is interesting to recall that while the Fowler commission insisted that the C.B.C. should be given a reasonable assurance of funds over a reasonable period of time for operational purposes, the commission opposed extending that period of time for capital development purposes. The minister must remember that in the report the commission says that the capital program of the C.B.C. can only be determined year by year, while the operating programs should be formulated four or five years ahead. This bill completely reverses that principle, and it is laid down that the capital program shall be considered for five years but the operating expenses covered by appropriations through parliament each year for one year only. And the corporation would have no other source of revenue except that derived through its commercial operations.
Then there is one final criticism which the minister would certainly expect me to make, and on which I have already touched in reference to other aspects of the bill. That is that this measure sets up a cumbersome and undesirably complicated machinery. I suggest to

Broadcasting
the minister that he and his colleagues have soon forgotten what they used to say in opposition about a multiplicity of boards and commissions as a solution for every government problem.
In the first place, as I have already said, these two boards and the way they will be reporting independently of each other to the minister may easily lead to conflict, confusion and duplication. As I have tried to point out, the Fowler commission warned specifically against that. The creation of these two boards is unnecessary, unwise and costly. Moreover-this will be the minister's problem; he has already indicated that it is a problem, as indeed it is-it may not be too easy to find 25 or 26 first-class people in Canada who are not connected with broadcasting, who are competent to deal with this highly complex field, and who are willing as unpaid members, except for expenses, to serve on these boards, except, of course, for the permanent members of the boards. That difficulty may be the more serious when we realize that with the type of legislation that is now proposed so much will depend on the kind of people who will compose these boards, as the minister himself has said.
The composition of these boards and especially that of the new board of broadcast governors raises certain other questions. The new board, as I understand it, will have two quite different functions to perform. The first and by far the most important will be to decide questions of policy and regulation and to hold hearings for that purpose. The second function will be to supervise broadcasting stations and to make sure that the regulations drafted by the board are being followed. In the opinion of the Fowler commission the first function would not be too burdensome, especially after the initial period, and would not take too much time of the board; while the second task, that of policing, could be quite effectively accomplished under the directives of the board by a competent and strong secretariat.
That is why the Fowler commission did not recommend that any member of the board should be full time. But the provisions of this bill are different from the recommendations contained in the report of the commission. Under clause 2 of the bill it is in fact being proposed that we have two distinct types of membership on the proposed board of broadcast governors. Three of them would be full time and ex-officio members of the executive committee, while the others would be part time and paid only when attending meetings of the board. Surely that will mean for practical purposes, and even if wide and skilled representation is provided, that the three full time members, one of whom

has no special position, are likely to become the czars of broadcasting in Canada, and will be in a special and privileged position to influence the decisions of the full board. The other members may not always, by the very nature of their relationship to the full time members, be in a position to prevent undesirable developments; because even with a large board three full time men who will be carefully selected by the government could exercise a profound influence on the future of broadcasting in this country.
In so far as the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is concerned the manner of the appointment of the new president and vicepresident in my view is a backward step, and it raises again the danger of political interference. Under the present act, and the minister will correct me if I am wrong, the chairman of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation holds office during good behaviour for a period of ten years, and he can be removed only by the governor in council for cause. In the proposed bill, and unlike the provisions governing the appointment of members of the board of broadcast governors, the president and vice-president of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation shall be appointed, and I quote from the bill-
-to hold office during pleasure for a period of seven years.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, they could be removed for reasons other than cause and without an address of the House of Commons and the other place. That applies to the president and vice president of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation under the proposed bill, but the minister will realize that also under this bill the other members of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation board can be removed only by an address of parliament. Why protect the security of tenure of the other directors of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation more carefully than that of the president and the vice president? Surely a sense of frustration and insecurity could quite easily develop because of this anomaly, which would affect the whole corporation in the knowledge that the two senior executives could be subject to the whims of a cabinet. That feeling of frustration and insecurity in the whole corporation could be increased by the knowledge that these two executives were appointed directly by the government, while today the general manager and the assistant general manager of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation are appointed by the government but only on the recommendation of the board of governors.
To sum up, Mr. Speaker, I feel that this bill is an uneasy and uncertain compromise between two points of view and, as is often the case, the effort to satisfy both points of

view has resulted in proposals that are not likely in the long run to satisfy either but might only weaken the essential principles on which a national broadcasting system has been built up in this country over the years. There is too much in this bill that is unclear. Above all, it is the kind of bill which should be given the most careful, complete and expert examination by a parliamentary committee, where experts from the varied interests concerned could appear and give their views not merely on the general principles involved but on the details of the bill itself; how it is likely to work out in practice; what are its defects; what are its advantages; what changes should be made to improve it.
This is a vitally important national question, that of broadcasting. The way to deal with it is not by a bill rushed through the house during the dying days of a long and exhausting session. This procedure, Mr. Speaker, is surely no recognition of those parliamentary rights or of that devotion to parliament which my hon. friends opposite talk about so often and at such length. For the benefit of the leader of the house, I may assure him that we will not support the second reading of this bill.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we felt considerable disappointment today at the brevity of the statement made by the Minister of National Revenue in introducing this bill. We felt that he failed to spell out government policy as fully as we thought we were entitled to have it on a bill as important as this. We feel, too, that the board of broadcast governors, when it is appointed as a result of this bill, will be looking to this debate, to statements by the minister and by other ministers, to learn what is the direction it should go in carrying out the very general outline of policies enumerated in the bill. If they cannot get it from this particular debate and from the statements of government ministers, it seems to me they will have to get it in discussions with the governor in council or with certain members of the government, and we wonder whether that will be the proper way in which the board of broadcast governors should decide what direction their policy is to take.
The bill states that the broadcasting regulations, as they now exist, will continue until 57071-3-257J
Broadcasting
changed by the board of broadcast governors. Well, if they are to change them, and I suggest the regulations do need changing, in what way are they to be changed? It does not seem to me that we get any indication of that from the minister's statement. We all have misgivings about the question of whether the regulations are going to be pro or anti private broadcasting or, if you wish to put it the other way, pro or anti C.B.C. We would like as a matter of fact-we cannot demand it, Mr. Speaker-to have a statement from the Prime Minister and from the Minister of Finance on their particular interest in this bill and what they conceive it to be.
We would not like to suggest, Mr. Speaker, that we do not have trust and confidence in the minister who has brought the measure before the house, but I think the whole atmosphere is filled with misgivings; I would suggest misgivings not only as expressed by the Leader of the Opposition, and expressed very well, but also misgivings among many of the members of the government party. We would like to know whether this bill is designed to improve and extend the national broadcasting system, or is it designed to lead to a gradual withering away of public broadcasting and the gradual taking over of broadcasting by the private broadcasters? Could we have a clear-cut statement on this particular point?
It seems to us that the whole speech of the Leader of the Opposition reflected misgivings as to the government's intentions. Maybe that is as it should be, since it is the duty of the opposition to express that misgiving, but we believe it is more than that. The central point of the speech of the Leader of the Opposition, as I understood it, was that a strong, independent public control of broadcasting is essential. Further than that, we cannot afford to lose control of this vital, cultural and non-material aspect of our life. For the C.C.F. I would say, in slang terms, you can double it in spades. We agree with that very strongly.
It was noticeable that in the speech of the Leader of the Opposition there were very few accolades for the private broadcasters. There was a certain amount of amusement there. We wondered what the Leader of the Opposition's alter egoes on the Winnipeg Free Press will think about that shortcoming in his speech. Of course we do not look upon it as a shortcoming.
We have had two fairly recent royal commissions looking into the whole broadcasting situation, and each of those commissions has found the private broadcasters wanting; each of those commissions has dynamited the main contention of the private broadcasters that

Broadcasting
they are supposedly hamstrung by the C.B.C. Those royal commissions have dynamited the whole idea fostered by the private stations and by those newspapers that are intimately connected with them, some of them in ownership terms, that there is an analogy between freedom of the press and freedom of the air. Each of the commissions has pointed out quite clearly that there is no logical support for this because of the limitations of the number of channels. Those royal commissions have pointed out that the private broadcasters have not been struggling against economic adversity; that when you look at the statistics as they were revealed in the chapter on private broadcasters I think any free enterpriser in the house will soon see what a wonderful investment those private stations have been. They have made a terrific amount of money and their net income after expenditure is, I would say, as high as in any kind of commercial operation we have in this country.
One of the other things the royal commissions have pointed out is that those private enterprisers are really neither free nor very enterprising. I ask the minister whether he subscribes to this comment, which is found at page 154 of the Fowler royal commission report:
We recommend that the board should insist on the improvement ot the programming of some private stations. We recommend further that the board should discharge its statutory duty of promoting and ensuring the greater use of Canadian talent by private stations with greater vigour than the board of governors has shown in the past.
Is that what the government wants this new board of broadcast governors to do? It is projected here. We would very much like to know. It is all very well for the private broadcasters to go around hollering that the C.B.C. provides unfair competition, and it is especially unfair because the C.B.C. is the taxpayers' agent. Where do they stand on competition? Well, as hon. members who followed the C.B.C. hearings know, we do not know of a single case where any private applicant came seeking a licence and was not opposed by private broadcasters who already had a licence in that particular field. Surely that very attitude shows how much they want competition.
One of the other things the Fowler royal commission brought out very clearly was whether the private broadcasters could afford to do much original programming. The report says at page 153:
It was suggested in evidence, and we believe it is generally assumed, that private broadcasters cannot afford to do much original programming or use much Canadian talent because the cost cannot be spread over several stations. Indeed this argument was advanced in one of the documents filed

by the C.A.R.T.B., although not discussed in evidence during the hearings. This assumption is, we believe, incorrect on two grounds. First, the financial results of a great many private radio and television stations, which we have examined, are quite good enough to permit these operators to do more original programming and to use more Canadian talent than they have done.
It is very clear that the Fowler commission did not trust the private stations and the private broadcasters. They did not go down the line with the private broadcasters; they turned them down. We want to know, and we still do not know from this government, whether it agrees with these general criticisms of the private broadcasters' position. If the government will state that it expects the board of broadcast governors to do something about the talent situation, to do something about getting higher standards on private stations, I think many of the misgivings we have would just evaporate, and we could assume that the government's intentions are the very best. We would like to know whether this bill is the augury of the victory of the private broadcasters. Does the government see it in that light, or is the bill a compromise designed to avoid making a hard decision? At several places in the bill there are provisions that the Canadian outlook should be supreme and that there should be high standards, but we wonder whether that is enough. Is this bill part of a real Canadian vision? We do not know. That is why we would like the Prime Minister and after him or almost co-equal with him, I suppose, the Minister of Finance to give us their views on the bill; because if there are misgivings I think that is where they generally settle at the present time.
As the Leader of the Opposition showed this morning, all the historical evidence, all reports of parliamentary committees and all reports of royal commissions that have studied the problem are in favour of a strong public system and public control of broadcasting. It is for that reason that a few of us feel, no matter what the intent may be, that when the board of broadcast governors is appointed the very same logic that led Mr. Fowler and his associates to take the position they did will lead the board of broadcast governors to recognize the strong need for control of the private broadcasters. A few of us feel that will likely happen, and we would like to know more about the government's intentions.
The Leader of the Opposition emphasized that we are now going to have two very clumsy boards. I think his suggestion, which is in line with the Fowler report, is very good; that we should cut down the membership of the C.B.C. board and have it report to the board of broadcast governors. What is

going to happen to the old C.B.C. board of governors? I should like the minister to tell us whether there is any thought of transferring some of its members to the board of broadcast governors in order to give some sort of continuity of ideas.
So far as the C.B.C. itself is concerned, we would like to know what is going to happen to the audience research section and the regulations section. We wonder how the board of broadcast governors can really carry out regulations, exercise control and have some idea of the standards of the private stations unless it does have an audience research section and a fairly substantial regulating section. The bill is not definitive enough to tell us what is going to happen.
A question has already been posed to the minister with respect to the conflict between the two boards. Which is going to win out? Which is going to wither away? Which is going to atrophy? As has been suggested, a lot will depend on the personnel. It would be quite possible to select as the three permanent members of the board of broadcast governors men of great drive and intent who could soon overshadow completely the directors of the C.B.C. Therefore it seems to me that the suggestion that the bill might be altered to have the C.B.C. report to the board of broadcast governors and thus dispense in a sense with the C.B.C. board of directors is worth considering, especially because of that conflict.
At the beginning of the minister's remarks he said that if necessary, if the opposition requested it, a committee would consider the bill at this session. We have not changed our attitude in that regard. We do not want a committee on this bill at this session, for somewhat the same reasons as the Leader of the Opposition advanced. We do not think the committee would have the time to do a very good job. I might also say that some of us wonder what the attitude of the large Conservative majority on such a committee would be, because we are not convinced that they know where the bill is leading.
The minister also went on to say that if it was requested a committee would be set up in the 1959 session to deal with this matter. We would then be considering an act rather than a bill. I would assume that we would have the opportunity to have the board of broadcast governors appear before us, and could consider the regulations they had spelled out up to that time. We think we would like to take advantage of that suggestion, but we would like to push it further and suggest that such a committee should meet every two years. Some people might even think it should meet every year, but
Broadcasting
in the past the general practice has been for such a committee to be set up every second year, on the average. We think there should be an undertaking in that regard so we will be able to follow fairly closely just what line the board is taking.
I should like to make one suggestion to the minister which is not covered by the bill in detail, yet must involve one of the most difficult problems the government must face and certainly the board of broadcast governors will have to face when looking for advice from the government. What are we going to do about the licencing of other television stations in the real plum market areas? One thinks of Toronto and of Mr. Bassett of the Telegram, Mr. Sedgwick of CFRB, Mr. Jack Kent Cooke of CKEY or some of the other people in that area who want television stations, and one wonders how the matter is going to be settled fairly.
I wonder whether the government has thought of suggesting to the board of broadcast governors anything like the independent television authority in England, where a corporation has been set up to provide programs, and advertisers go to that corporation to buy their programs rather than purchasing them through their own advertising agencies. One thing such an independent television authority would do would be to end the pressure which I am sure the government is under at the present time and which the board of broadcast governors will be under, as to who is going to get the plum.
Dissatisfaction with the financing aspects of the bill was revealed at least partially in an editorial this morning by a Toronto newspaper that usually strongly supports the government. The suggestion they make is one that we feel is good, that the financing should be put on a better long-term basis. I notice that there is provision in the bill for the capital program of the corporation to be submitted to the government once every five years. I cannot see why plans could not be made for a five-year period and brought up to date at the end of every year. We would then always have a five-year projection before us. That may be too often, but it is pretty difficult to go along with the once every five years provision.
One reason why many of us in remote constituencies are interested in this matter is that we would like to get some sort of timetable with respect to when the C.B.C. is going to establish radio relay and television satellite stations in our constituencies which will provide coverage for the people on the fringe who at the present time are not getting either radio or television broadcasts. A financing set-up based upon a five-year program that

Broadcasting
would be projected each year would be much better than the set-up now suggested.
Fears were expressed by the Leader of the Opposition about the role of the Minister of Finance with respect to financing, and the fact that he would have a power and authority which perhaps would be unfortunate for the steady growth of the C.B.C. Again we have the very same misgivings about that particular gentleman, though perhaps they are based more upon the particular gentleman than would be the case if someone else were holding the office.
There is one point that always comes up in any discussion of broadcasting. We are told by newspaper people and particularly radio people that the private stations are giving the people what they want. I think it has been decided by some of the best people in the country who have looked into the problem closely that what the thinking people of the country want is a public system that has a national bias and a national interest, something that extends right across the country.
The point, which was well made in this debate, that private broadcasters tend to concentrate upon local and regional rather than national interests is quite obvious. We know where the rich market areas are and we know where the poor market areas are. You can be sure it is not the intention of the private broadcasters to ever get themselves trapped into the kind of national network broadcasts that will have them doing work in those areas from which they cannot get a good financial return. The whole question is, are they to be allowed to concentrate networks in those rich market areas to the disadvantage of our public organization, in this case the C.B.C.?
We do not know what the government's intentions are. There could very well be a kind of regional network, composed of private broadcasting stations, set up under this legislation which would siphon off all the cream from national advertising revenues and leave the C.B.C. with a fantastically expensive role which would give poor coverage to the less attractive areas. Before this group votes either for or against this bill we want more information as to the intent of the government with regard to this particular measure. We reiterate our trust in the minister's attitude, especially as that trust has been reinforced by the three forthright statements he has made in this house. We have further misgivings, however, in connection with this bill. Before this debate closes let us hear from the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister as to what vision they have for our national broadcasting set-up. If that is done

we will be able to make our decision on the vote on second reading in a much more intelligent fashion.
We trust that when the bill goes to committee the minister will be agreeable to certain minor amendments, or that he may be interested in having some minor amendments made in the bill and especially in those clauses relating to the C.B.C. The attitude of this party has always been strongly in favour of the C.B.C.; as a matter of fact sometimes I have thought so strongly in favour that we have allowed ourselves to miss some of the weaknesses of the C.B.C. I believe the primary weakness we have missed has been that the C.B.C. did not really regulate the private broadcasters in regard to advertising to even the standards that could be applied without any qualitative judgment.
Our position is essentially the same. We believe in a very strong public broadcasting set-up, and that it is in our national interests. We suspect we will never get anything like that from the private broadcasters of this country. We feel that the whole position of the private broadcasters has been exploded by two royal commissions. We would like assurance from the government at this time, in this debate, that they agree the bill is not a victory for the private broadcasters but that it represents a victory for national broadcasting in the public interest.
