subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a most important debate. It deals not only with the informing and educating of the public, but also with cultural matters in general.
I therefore trust that it will not be considered out of place for a member with quite a lot of experience in education to take part in this debate. I do so in a completely nonpartisan spirit for I believe it would be wrong to rouse sectional differences in a matter which calls for respect of principles and utter impartiality.
I am delighted that this new legislation on broadcasting has been introduced. It is what most people wanted. It gives expression to the representations of various undertakings, bodies and public organizations of every nature which have probed into the broadcasting question from a national point of view and which have made their opinions known. Thus, in introducing this bill, the government shows the importance it attaches to

popular opinion. Alter having aroused public interest and questioned people from all walks of life, the government is today introducing a bill based on excellent recommendations from all sides, especially the Fowler commission; but it is the government which initiated the bill. It will not come as a surprise, therefore, if I express my satisfaction to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan).
The problem of Canadian broadcasting has been in the limelight for a long time, and several commissions have gone into the matter on different occasions. Various systems have been tried out, and an attempt was made to set up a regulatory body which would allow of government-controlled broadcasting side by side with private station networks. What was necessary was, on the one hand, to make sure that there would be no invasion by the influential American broadcasting organizations-this by setting up a government-controlled national network-and, on the other hand, to still extend a welcoming hand to private enterprise. That is how Canada has come to have government-controlled radio operating side by side with numerous independent stations.
I do not think the coming of television has altered the basic elements of the problem; it has simply magnified the problem and made it more intricate. All that has happened is that the difficulties encountered by our national broadcasting system have continued, but on a larger scale. What we have to do now is to devise, for the former problems, solutions which allow for the new factors. And these solutions must be based on the principle which, from the very start, guided those who built up our broadcasting system: I mean the balance that must be struck between a government broadcasting agency and broadcasting by private stations.
I do not intend to retrace the stages of development of our national broadcasting system which resulted in the setting up of the C.B.C. mechanism entrusted with supervision of both government-controlled and privately-owned broadcasting. Suffice it to emphasize that it was eventually felt to be difficult for the C.B.C. to be both judge and litigant in some matters involving the interests of both government-controlled broadcasting and broadcasting by private stations. It was purely and simply a matter of devising a solution which would satisfy those who asked for more independence for private networks, hand in hand with closer supervision by the C.B.C.
When all is said and done, the object of all those who put pressure on the government was not to introduce a completely new look in the broadcasting system obtaining up to now, but to modernize it so that it will
Broadcasting
change with the times, and to widen the scope it offers to private enterprise.
Even a cursory study of the bill will show that it involves no aggressive designs. The whole essence of this act is that it should perfect our broadcasting system. It is an attempt at an answer, a solution (subject to oher improvements) to the problem of supervision.
That is just where the state comes in-to ensure that supervision. Nobody denies it that right. Whether you consider radio and television as a source of information, whether you turn it into an instrument of education or culture, you must necessarily concede that its activities call for supervision.
For a long time, it has been recognized that it would not be good for the government-that is to say, the Canadian parliament-to directly control broadcasting. Political interference could pave the way to certain abuses on which I need not dwell. However, no one can imagine a regulatory body absolutely independent of parliament and in no way answerable for its administration. We must also take into consideration the twofold problem of state broadcasting and broadcasting by private stations. The experience of the C.B.C. proves that it is not easy for such an agency to control both its own operations and those of similar agencies whose interests conflict with its own. Moreover, state-controlled radio broadcasting cannot be absolutely independent of parliament; it cannot provide its own regulations, nor can it rely to that end on private stations.
It is therefore necessary to set up, at the intermediate level, a regulatory body distinct from but answerable to parliament, an agency independent of both a public agency and private radio and T.V. stations. A body such as this has been advocated in virtually all various recommendations submitted to the Canadian government for quite some time.
Through this bill, the Minister of National Revenue is setting up that regulatory body. The bill, which sets out all the legal aspects of that new institution, emphasizes the need for a balance between a state agency and private stations for the broadcasting of radio and television.
As will have been noted, the bill also provides for the reorganization of the C.B.C. It has been emphasized, and rightly, that the government has no intention, as shown by the terms of the act, to revamp the C.B.C. from top to bottom.

Broadcasting
To put it simply, it will be governed by the new board of broadcast governors. An administrative body is being established, similar to the previous one, except that its functions are limited to the operations of the corporation for which it is designed.
The fact that the government does not radically change the C.B.C. has been favourably commented upon by the press in general. At most, a very few cautious remarks have been made about the fate of the present management of the corporation. The thing to do in this case, Mr. Speaker, is to trust the government, as should be done in the case of all our democratic institutions, which are based above all, on the confidence given those who are entrusted with the responsibility of government, at any level.
Besides, the legislation clearly defines the duties of the C.B.C.'s high officials. On the other hand, it is based on the general principle of serving, in all respects, the common good. It is in such a context that it is important to judge the actions of all those who will take part in the operations of government-sponsored broadcasting. There is absolutely nothing ambiguous in such an attitude. We would be ill-advised to charge anyone with malevolent intentions.
In the final analysis, only those who feel guilty in some way would have any reasons to fear. It is in this sense that, speaking of the Liberals, a journalist of Le Droit wrote, last Saturday, and I quote:
They begin to realize that there is such a thing as C.B.C. "monopoly" over the broadcasting of news, as well as over the broadcasting of national and international news on television; that this monopoly places present C.B.C. officials in a delicate position with regard to the new leaders of the federal government; that freedom of speech will become a sinister farce unless there is a change in the present system and unless private television stations in the larger cities are granted the right to use commentators other than those picked by ministers, by ministers' representatives, or representatives of ministers' representatives of today or of yesterday.
The government's intention therefore consists in meeting the wishes of the taxpayers by providing the country with an adequate broadcasting system. The government thinks that the popular will has sufficiently expressed itself in this regard to believe that it is necessary to satisfy its legitimate requests. I do not see why the adoption of some legislation which would meet the views of the great majority of our citizens should be postponed. There is talk of creating a committee, and all kinds of reasons are given to postpone the passage of this bill.

The political intention of such tactics will fool no one. The problem of broadcasting is not new, and members of the opposition have had sufficient time to think ahead of the changes which they might wish to suggest about this new legislation. All their speeches show that they are merely marking time, and the hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) showed it this morning. He has developed a lengthy theory-not a novel one either-which can be interpreted as an indirect encroachment upon the rights of private radio and television broadcasting.
I insisted on the problem of regulation, Mr. Speaker, as an essential factor of this bill. I kept strictly to the general principle and to its concrete juridical formulation. I would now like to speak briefly on some aspects of the current procedure to be followed in administering this legislation.
Broadcasting regulations call for some standards of action and clear basic principles, besides those aiming at the common welfare of this country and its citizens. I shall leave the care of discussing the technical aspects of C.B.C. financing to other hon. members, Mr. Speaker. I shall merely discuss the regulations, in so far as they affect the general administration of broadcasting and programs.
The necessity to be aware of exactly how considerable a part broadcasting plays in the field of public information and general education cannot be stressed enough. It may be said today that a citizen may very well be what broadcasting makes him. His political and social attitude will be conditioned by everything that comes out of this marvellous gadget, which has become an indispensable companion in each home. The television screen is at the same time the mirror of the world and an intimate counsellor. It has to provide recreation. It is also asked to give directions. It is expected to have the answers to all sorts of questions. In any case, it brings the latest concepts in our minds and is largely a guide to our way of life.
We certainly remember the apprehension once caused to educators and politicians by the appearance of radio and the development of American networks. People feared the worst for our Canadian civilization. This healthy fright gave us our national network and our government-controlled broadcasting.
I think the promoters of that movement should be commended. They have tried in good faith to preserve us from a too strong influence of United States civilization. At the same time they created a government body of a quality we can hardly praise too highly.

It is however important to keep in mind today the principles that have inspired the creators of our national broadcasting.
It was first of all intended to provide public information. Thus we may hear and observe the world by radio and television, as a means of communication. It tends to inform citizens about the way of life of mankind in the world and in the community of which we are a part. It does fulfil a task of the highest importance which calls for the strictest honesty and complete impartiality.
On the other hand broadcasting indirectly plays another and quite as essential part as educator in the social, civic, political, religious, artistic and other fields. In this respect, its leading principles must be perfectly adjusted. They must be based on an accurate awareness of natural law which clearly defines good and evil, truth and untruth. They have to reflect the philosophy of our western and Christian civilization.
Furthermore, I cannot see that radio or television shed a single one of these fundamental responsibilities just because they are providing people with fun and amusement. Radio and T.V. must avoid, like the plague, anything which could totally or only partially detract from the morals of viewers or listeners, or anything which would end up by impairing their intellectual and moral standards and which would prevent them from being men in the most perfect sense of the word, and-above all-from being public-minded citizens.
Those are the sort of principles which must lie at the basis of any properly inspired working of our national radio and television programs.
In this connection we must remember the original intent of the promoters of radio broadcasting.
I would like to return to this matter at a time when, through new legislative action, Canadian broadcasting is being reorganized. It must not be forgotten that radio and television are instruments placed at the disposal of society with a view to serving its needs. That is their purpose. Their only object is to assist the citizens of the country in their individual or community life. It is not superfluous to insist on that point at a time when we are often tempted to forget that technical progress is not an end in itself, but that it must serve to improve man's living conditions and personal standards.
A moment ago I mentioned the importance which the new legislation ascribes to private enterprise in the field of radio and T.V. broadcasting. This implies a survey of the particular conditions of broadcasting. Every effort must be made to ensure both the development of
Broadcasting
independent radio and television stations and to raise the average standard on those networks. It would be regrettable if private networks multiplied programs which would not be up to the standards of those carried by the government-owned network. True, the position of private stations is often made difficult by the fact that they must rely very heavily on "commercials". It is all the more to their credit that they nevertheless manage to broadcast programs which provide the listener with wholesome entertainment, and full factual information, although there is room for a great deal of improvement in this regard. I wish to insist upon this point that a very special effort should be made to restore to an even degree the Canadian character of private station broadcasting, too often a replica of American broadcasting. In fact, with all due regard to circumstances, we should require from private stations the same standard of broadcasting required at this time from the government-owned system.
Let me emphasize that I am not attempting to pillory anyone. These are merely personal observations with regard to the position of private broadcasting. I am merely pointing out some weaknesses which must not be allowed to develop further but which, on the contrary, must disappear as private networks are extended. I know most of the private stations in our province. I am convinced that their broadcasts are of a fairly high standard. May I be allowed in this connection to point to the excellent work performed by the stations at Roberval, Alma, Jonquiere and Chicoutimi which have done everything possible to produce high quality programs. I believe that the same must hold true of all the other private stations in our province.
It would be well, at this point, to refer to the problem of personnel in radio and T.V. stations. While I know that technical employees are selected with the greatest care,- I refer here to those who are charged with the responsibility of handling radio and T.V. transmission equipment,-I fail to see why equal care should not be taken with regard to selecting the people actually in charge of programs, programming and presentation. It is high time our radio and T.V. stations shut their doors on those people, neither technically nor professionally trained, who have been performing duties requiring wide general knowledge, a reasonable amount of culture and a definite sense of taste, for which they are utterly unprepared. I realize that, at the beginning, it was not easy to decide or to enact laws on the professional ability of radio and television producers and performers. This experimental stage had to be gone through.

Broadcasting
I believe the time has come to require from radio and television professionals what could be called a certificate of ability or proficiency, that is to say an official recognition in the form of a certificate issued by an institution, a conservatory or a university, the recognition of a certain amount of knowledge, of technological training for an immediate career in this field. Some institutions have begun to offer courses to that end. They seek a formula for a training course for announcers, newscasters, or radio and T.V. commentators. Also considered are courses in language and composition, for radio and television script writers. Our broadcasting system is old enough, has given enough proof of its vitality, for us to demand high standards for admission into professional radio and television, especially as there is no shortage of applicants.
Many young people are attracted by a career which in itself is highly interesting and fairly well paid. They are often motivated by a desire for easy success without the necessity of much training. I do not want to be misunderstood. I am not saying that most radio and television professionals are lacking in culture. But I believe that some of them lack immediate and specific training. We have the pleasure of seeing and hearing, especially on the government network, professional performers who give the best example of careful training and concern for perfection which make them outstanding stars. Those are the qualifications that should be required from the majority of people who aspire to a career in that field. I hope that radio and television schools will be established, and also institutions to train people for the careers of announcer, reporter or commentator. Then, it would be possible to lay down rules and require a certificate of proficiency, just as a certificate is required from school teachers. Of course, this problem would have to be studied and left to the consideration of experts who could determine regulations to that effect.
In the same line of thought, I should like to point out one provision of section XI of the new bill whereby the board may make regulations:
-for promoting and ensuring the greater use of Canadian talent by broadcasting stations.
This provision is not unnecessary. Not that Canadian artists have been refused access to radio and television broadcasting, but I believe that there is room for improvement in

that respect. Our radio and television stations are to be commended for inviting, on occasion, foreign performers of international reputation. On the other hand, they should not make a practice of offering refuge to third-rate performers, discredited in their own country or who have not managed to reach a high level of artistic achievement. We have in Canada many high-grade performers. We also have many young people of great promise in this field. Our radio and television broadcasting should serve to encourage this young talent. I know that this has been done, as witness the well-known programs of Singing Stars of Tomorrow, Futures etoiles and, more recently, of the Couronne d'or.
To avoid too many a flower being "born to blush unseen," to avoid some artists monopolizing program time, to avoid favouritism, there should be competitions to determine the candidates' suitability for television and radio. Here again, through competitions, experts should act as judges.
To remain in the field of Canadian talent, the C.B.C. is known to make abundant use of the resources of Canadian writers, except perhaps that it displays towards some of them a sympathy which somewhat transforms them into permanent employees of the C.B.C. I refer to writers of serial stories which for 10, 15 and even 20 years, have been featured over the C.B.C. I believe this is encouraging a form of facility which is fatal to writing talent, and stifling wholesome rivalry or emulation which would be beneficial to the writers themselves if they were obliged to break new ground, under competition from younger writers. It may be argued that the listeners and viewers are clamouring for programs which have become fixtures on our national broadcasting network. It seems to me that those requests could be satisfied just the same if programs were varied from time to time. In addition to giving other writers a chance of showing what they can do, it would prevent some programs, which were undoubtedly very popular at the start, to stretch themselves into vacuity or vapid repetition.
There would be room too, in this field, for a process of competition or contests. Greater interest would be thus stimulated which would promote and foster artistic endeavour.
The danger which threatens this type of institution is monopoly, unconscious monopoly appearing as a result of certain circumstances and which finally becomes glaringly

obvious to detached observers. In this connection, it might perhaps be appropriate, in this appraisal of our national broadcasting system, to recall certain standards that the C.B.C. had established for itself, and that Mr. Raymond David, of the C.B.C., emphasized at the meeting of the 34th Social Week of Canada.
Speaking of public information, Mr. David said the following:
In this important sector of public affairs too. the program division had, since its inception, to comply with the principles set down in the white paper of the corporation and to continue operating according to the following principles:
1.	The airwaves belong to the people, who have the right to hear the main points of view on all questions of importance.
2.	The airwaves should not be controlled by individuals or influential groups by reason of their material resources or their particular position.
3.	The right of rejoinder is inherent to the democratic rule of freedom of speech.
4.	Freedom of speech and the free exchange of opinions are the two guardian principles of institutional freedom.
That, Mr. Speaker, is the true code defining the proper ethics of information and of the exchange of ideas which are so frequently broadcast. It is proper briefly to review each of those points.
1.	The airwaves belong to the people who have the right to hear the main points of view on all questions of importance.
This rule prohibits any controlled one-sided information, which does not leave full liberty of judgment to the listener, because he has only been told one angle of the issue and only been shown one aspect of the picture. It would moreover suggest a dialogue, a free exchange of opinions. Because, if an audience has to be informed, it must be given the means to get an accurate and complete knowledge of the facts.
2.	The airwaves should not be controlled by individuals or influential groups, by reason of their resources or their particular position.
What was intended by that was the elimination of monopolies based on financial or political power.
3.	The right of rejoinder is inherent in the democratic doctrine of freedom of speech.
This aspect is very important. It deals with the right of citizens and institutions of not being convicted without trial. It involves the easy and efficient use of the right of attack and rejoinder. This excludes trials without evidence and convictions in absentia.
4.	Freedom of speech and the free exchange of opinions are the two basic guarantees of freedom of institutions.
This fourth point summarizes all the others. It is a kind of charter of freedom of expression.
Broadcasting
Without any pretense at instituting a trial in due form, one may ask if radio and television have respected the provisions of this charter in our country.
We are led to believe that there may be some reason to reconsider the whole question in the light of principles formerly laid down by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, in view of the absence of dialogue in the very field of criticism of our institutions, of some form of controlled information in the field of politics, of an apparent set purpose of disparagement of particular groups of citizens, of the too negative aspect of some claims, of ungracious insistence upon stressing the real or fancied wrongs and foibles of the political administration.
There are all sorts of ways of intruding upon consciences. Not the least dangerous is that which would consist in remaining silent in the face of the positive achievements of a particular system while, at the same time, laying stress on all its possible weaknesses. There is no justification either for making a permanent comparison between social, economic and educational conditions in one particular province, as compared to those of another province, to the detriment of the former.
I am reminded here of the very appropriate remarks of Monseigneur Paul-Emile Gosselin of Quebec city who, speaking of the government owned broadcasting system at the 34th Social Week of Canada, stated:
We do not believe however that state-owned radio and television give total or faithful expression to national feeling in French Canada. Perfection is difficult of attainment in a field such as this. Without entering into discussions which would appear to be pointless, let us merely express the hope that each and every school of national thought may find some means of expressing itself through these official media. To achieve this result, those entrusted with programming should be broad-minded enough to admit that some people may not share their own particular views on controversial matters and that there are sincere patriots, with a knowledge of present day issues, outside the small select circles they frequent.
Mr. Speaker, that is one of the most difficult problems we have to deal with in respect of broadcasting in this country. Any form of intellectual monopoly is odious and contrary to the right of the people to hear "all main points of view on any important issue", to quote a phrase formerly employed by the responsible people in the C.B.C. Under cover of a mission of intellectual, social or political liberation, no one has the right to attempt to enforce his own views on others nor to make a national system of his own peculiar beliefs or convictions in any particular area. A fundamental right rooted in natural law is thus

Broadcasting
violated. It is especially wrong to misuse the public system in an attempt to force individuals to accept one's particular faith, intellectual, social, political, or religious. Mr. Raymond David, whom I quoted a moment ago, expressed that same conviction when he said:
-radio and television are not and must not become a forum for the propagandists of a given school of thought, but must remain open to all opinions held acceptable by our democratic society in general. They must, and that is their main task, allow listeners to become familiar, on any topic, with the various trends of opinion which, together, make up what is called public opinion,
Mr. Speaker, I hope that the new board of governors will uphold that essential freedom of thought and expression when assuming its regulatory functions over broadcasting by both public and private stations. We are confident that it will discharge this duty so as to preserve the present high standards of public broadcasting and so as to correct what must be corrected and improve what must be improved in the fields of both public and private broadcasting. It must exercise over the C.B.C. as well as over private stations a discreet but firm supervision so as to prevent any form of monopoly. As far as the C.B.C. is concerned, it seems to us that the emphasis must be laid on decentralizing and on favouring all public radio and television stations in all areas of this country.
Mr. Speaker, this legislation, which will soon be enacted, is perhaps not complete nor perfect but, as I said at the beginning of my remarks, we must have confidence in the government whose sole aim is to provide for the good functioning of our institutions and which, by this bill on Canadian broadcasting, is implementing the recommendations put forward by various commissions and by organizations that have been dealing for a very long time with problems connected with broadcasting. To delay the adoption of this legislation would deprive our citizens of their right to a continuing improvement of our Canadian radio and television system.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is most unfortunate that the government has waited until almost the last minute of this session to introduce this very important bill. It is unfair to parliament and to the people of Canada. In the speech from the throne the government promised to set up a select committee on broadcasting, which it did not do. It would have been the proper course to follow. This committee would have
[Mr. Tremblay. 1
studied carefully all aspects of the legislation on broadcasting; it would have called witnesses and informed the members of all aspects of radio and television, and today we would have been in a better position to deal with this bill. Instead of doing that the government decided to put before us at the very end of the session Bill C-55, respecting broadcasting. I want to take a few moments, Mr. Speaker, to discuss the merits of this bill. At the end of my remarks I propose to move an amendment.
In past years I have expressed my opinion in this house as to the advisability of setting up a regulatory body. What I had in mind at that time was a body similar to the one proposed by the Fowler commission, nothing more, and I am still in favour of it. Instead of doing that the government brings forward a major change in the structure of our broadcasting system in Canada. The bill before us today provides for the creation of broadcasting governors, whose objects and purposes are set out in section 10 of the bill, and I quote:
The board shall, for the purpose of ensuring the continued existence and efficient operation of a national broadcasting system and the provision of a varied and comprehensive broadcasting service of a high standard that is basically Canadian in content and character, regulate the establishment and operation of networks of broadcasting stations, the activities of public and private broadcasting stations in Canada and the relationship between them and provide for the final determination of all matters and questions in relation thereto.
There will be two distinct boards, and if we read carefully sections 10, 29 and 36, we see that the powers given to each board may overlap one another. The two bodies will be responsible to parliament, to a member of the cabinet. I contend, Mr. Speaker, that this arrangement will be very difficult to work out. Instead of doing that the government should have followed the Fowler commission's recommendations to the effect that there should be only one Canadian broadcasting governing board to which the C.B.C. would be required to report.
If this bill is accepted it will mean the end of the long-accepted principle that the Canadian broadcasting system is a single system made up of both privately-owned and publicly-owned stations under the control of a single agency responsible to parliament. The proposed bill only seems to add to the confusion, while the aim of the Fowler commission was to clarify the responsibility and eliminate the confusion which had come to exist under the present legislation. As stated

in an editorial which appeared in the Ottawa Journal on August 21:
The responsibility for a national service should be clearly enumerated by the government. Otherwise there is danger of overlapping, misunderstanding and inefficiency.
The bill before us rejects the Fowler commission's advice that:
In broadcasting it is of primary importance that the operating agency be independent of control and interference from the government of the day.
The commission goes on to say:
Since in our constitutional practice, money bills must originate from the government, annual votes give to the executive an almost constant vehicle for influence, or the appearance of influence on broadcasting agency.
In an article in the Ottawa Citizen on August 22 by Mr. Frank Swanson, the following appeared:
Parliament and the government will now hold the control of the C.B.C.'s purse-strings which in the eyes of many people, could be a threat to the independence of thought and action by the C.B.C.
This brings me to the method of financing the C.B.C. under the new bill. Here is what the Globe and Mail has to say about it, and I quote from an editorial which appeared on August 25:
But how hesitant these measures are, and how vague! They ask the C.B.C. to plan five years in advance and to get its plans approved, but offer no assurance that approval, once given, will be backed up by cash. They do not even specify that the annual budgets be drawn up or considered within the framework of the five-year plans. They do nothing, really, but perpetuate the unsatisfactory arrangement whereby the C.B.C. goes to Ottawa every year, cap in hand, asking for money-an arrangement which not only invites inefficiency in its operations, but begs political interference in its affairs.
The method of financing the C.B.C., as proposed in the bill, is an open invitation to political interference. It was the operating phase of the C.B.C. which the Fowler commission wanted to protect against the everpresent threat of government interference. That was one of the primary reasons why the commission recommended a single board of governors and that the C.B.C. be responsible to parliament for its finances as well as its activities through the board of broadcast governors.
Under the existing legislation the operating personnel of the C.B.C., the general manager and below, are insulated from direct political pressure and interference by the presence of the board of governors and a full-time chairman. Now that insulation will be removed. The minister will now deal directly with the senior officers of the corporation instead of with an officer removed from day-to-day operations.
Broadcasting
I do not want to imply that the present minister to whom the C.B.C. now reports will personally interfere in the business of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, but after listening in this house not so very long ago to the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon), I feel that the matter has to be brought up at this time. In his speech delivered on July 14, the hon. member said, as reported at page 2228 of Hansard:
A clean-up job is necessary in the C.B.C.
Mr. Robert Rumilly, a well-known Union Nationale active supporter, has been asking for a clean-up regularly in the Union Nationale paper, Nouvelles Illustrees; so has the Union Nationale official daily, the Montreal Matin, in an editorial which appeared on July 19. Knowing for a fact what the Union Nationale people have in mind when they talk about a clean-up, I am afraid that if there were any possibility for them to do so they would fire all those who do not share their political views in order to replace them by political supporters. It would be terrible if the fascists like Robert Rumilly, Adrien Arcand and others like them played important parts in the operations of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
I know that since the election of the Progressive Conservative party pressure has been put on the C.B.C. by Union Nationale supporters to fire certain people in the C.B.C. Even the member to whom I referred earlier has suggested in the house that at least three people be fired on the alleged accusation that they were leftists. The hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm has never given us a definition of what he calls a leftist. As far as I know, all those who do not share Mr. Duplessis' views are leftists. I know for a fact that at least one person mentioned by the hon. member on that occasion is a strong supporter of the Liberal party and I do not think that that reason would be sufficient to fire him in order to replace him by Mr. Rumilly or Mr. Arcand. This is the kind of political interference which should never exist in a corporation like the C.B.C.
The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is a public service paid for by the Canadian people and nothing should prevent the corporation from discharging its responsibilities to the satisfaction of the Canadian public. There should never be interference such as I referred to a few moments ago. The C.B.C. should never be an instrument in the hands of politicians. I am sure that neither the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) nor the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker)

Broadcasting
would tolerate that the French C.B.C. networks at least should be controlled by the premier of Quebec and his friends. I am sure that the Minister of National Revenue and the Prime Minister want the C.B.C. to be free of any political interference. That is why I submit respectfully to the minister that any section in the bill which would bring about an opening for political interference should be amended. I respectfully submit to the minister that the C.B.C., instead of having to report to parliament, should report to the board of broadcast governors which in turn would report to parliament.
Section 10 of the bill gives power to the Board of broadcast governors to regulate the establishment and operation of networks of broadcasting stations, the activities of public and private broadcasting stations in Canada and the relationship between them and provide for a final determination of all matters and questions in relation thereto. How can the board of broadcast governors regulate all these matters and provide for their final determination when it has nothing to do with the financing of the C.B.C. and is not able to check on the financial operations of the corporation? Again I submit that the corporation should report through the board of governors and that, radio broadcasting being part of the public domain, private broadcasters should equally report to the board of governors.
I want to stress the fact that the two boards described by the bill will certainly get in each other's hair and in a case of conflict it would seem to me that the C.B.C. board would be placed in an inferior position. The C.B.C. now becomes an agent of the crown in such a manner that it will not be able to maintain its independence. If the bill is adopted without amendment it is my view that it will be very difficult for the C.B.C. to operate.
Not only should there have been provision, as I said earlier in my remarks, for the C.B.C. to report to the board of broadcast governors but the C.B.C. should have had assurance of long range financing. The Fowler commission recommended annual grants to the corporation with a review after five years. Instead, section 35 provides for the corporation to lay annually before parliament through its minister a capital budget and an operating budget which means, in other words, that the corporation will have to come each year to parliament and beg for its financing.
The proposed method of financing hampers the management of the corporation in planning its operations over a reasonable period of time. While the government may argue that the bill provides for the corporation to

have working capital in the amount of $6 million and that its debt to the government in excess of that amount will be extinguished, this money cannot be spent on operating expenses.
The failure to provide the corporation with an assured income for operating expenses places the future growth and development of the corporation in jeopardy. If expenditures increase, as they most certainly will, and the corporation requests ever-increasing sums from the government, the government could conceivably reject the requests on the grounds that the federal treasury could not afford it in view of other, more urgent expenditures. The public might accept the government's view without too great protest, regardless of how valid the corporation's claims were. In other words, the government may now, without any public protest, starve the C.B.C. financially. This is an unfair burden to place upon management.
I should like to deal briefly with another aspect of the bill. Section 19 provides for the board of broadcast governors to report to parliament through a member of the cabinet designated by the governor in council. Section 36, on the other hand, provides for the C.B.C. to report to parliament through a minister designated again by the governor in council.
It can happen that the two bodies will have to report to two different cabinet ministers. What will happen then in case of conflict? There can be cause for ministerial conflict which would hamper the work of the C.B.C. and of the board of broadcast governors. If the two boards are going to be established by the government, the bill should contain a clause by which the two boards should be responsible to the same minister. If the government is going to rush this legislation through, it should be very careful as to who is going to be appointed to the two boards.
In studying the present legislation Mr. Frank Swanson, in the Ottawa Citizen of August 22 last, asked the question, "how will it work", and gave this answer:
In the end, it probably will depend primarily on the quality and abilities of the men who will make up the new board of broadcast governors.
In my own judgment the bill will not satisfy anyone. In an editorial which appeared in the Toronto Star on August 20 last I find the following:
Canadians have a right to expect that federal broadcasting legislation will, so far as possible, guarantee three things:	(1) A strong national
broadcasting system; (2) freedom of this system from political interference; (3) responsible use of the channels and frequencies which private broadcasters are privileged to occupy.

The bill which the Diefenbaker government has just put before parliament guarantees none of these things.

I was wondering if the minister wished to reply to this amendment? In that case, since there seems to be no one else who wishes to speak at the moment, there are a few observations on the amendment itself I should like to make, and a few on the bill, which I think justify the presentation of the amendment which the hon. member for Dollard (Mr. Rouleau) has just presented. He has, of course, simply done in a formal way what the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson)
Broadcasting
did informally in his appeal to the government this morning, which I am sure the Leader of the Opposition expected would have been accepted without a formal vote of the house. The hon. member has moved that this bill be not proceeded with at this session, but that it be presented at the next session or a better bill introduced on another occasion.
It does seem to me that the arguments which we made on this side of the house at the resolution stage, that this bill should be given first reading and should be left for study by hon. members during the recess and for study by the public generally, are amply justified by our examination of the bill itself. In the first place, the bill does not live up to the advance notice which, I admit, was in rather vague terms. I am not accusing the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) of misleading the house deliberately, but I must admit that he misled me, and I think he misled a good many others in the country into thinking what the government was going to do was substantially to implement the recommendations of the Fowler report. It is true, and I want to be quite fair about this, that the minister did indicate, in response to a specific question I asked at the resolution stage, that the financial scheme would not be what was recommended in the Fowler report. I must say, from that moment on, I began to have very grave doubts about what we were likely to see in the bill. When we got the bill we saw it was a great deal worse than anything I had feared.
I want to make the same points as the Leader of the Opposition has about some of the respects in which the bill seems to me to be worse. While I really do not think I have any new points to add to those made by the Leader of the Opposition, there are some aspects of those points that he made so comprehensively this morning which I do believe deserve to be underlined. Before doing that, I should like to take up the challenge of the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher), and say that I am more interested in the views expressed by the Free Press in its great days than I am in its later expressions of opinion on this subject. I assure Your Honour, lest there be any doubt about this, that the editorial I now propose to quote has been quoted many times before in parliament and has no relationship to the present bill or proceedings before the house, although it has a direct bearing on the subject matter of the present bill. The most recent occasion on which this article was quoted in this house was July 14, 1958. It has to do, of course,

Broadcasting
with that great stage in the history of broadcasting in Canada when Mr. Bennett introduced the Canadian radio commission legislation in 1932. At that time, the editor of the Free Press had this to say:
The radio issue now being decided at Ottawa is quite simple and very easily grasped. There is a choice between a national system and the handing over of the radio-supporting public of Canada to the radio monopolies of the United States. All the pleas put forth on behalf of private control of radio in Canada, no matter how plausibly presented, nor how strongly backed by eminent figures in the world of finance, are in support of a system which, in its practical working out will make Canada a subordinate annex of the United States radio-land and give the final (if concealed) voice in the decisions of how radio is to be operated in Canada to purely commercial interests, American in character.
The day of the small detached and supposedly independent radio station is about over in Canada. If the field is left to private enterprise, there will be rapid consolidation of these stations into a combination. We shall have a privately-owned monopoly of the air, and this monopoly will operate in harmony with the great radio monopoly of the United States-the harmony that always exists between the boss that gives orders and the dependent subordinate who obeys them.
I knew the late Mr. Dafoe very well, and that, of course, is just the way he talked. I think Mr. Dafoe was fundamentally right in the first paragraph he wrote but in the light of experience in the recent past, I do not believe I would say he was entirely right in the first sentence of the second paragraph. He said:
The day of the small detached and supposedly Independent radio station is about over in Canada.
I think it is a very happy and fortunate circumstance that he has been proved to be wrong about that one point. I think the small, detached and independent radio station owned by someone in a local community in Canada has performed an increasingly useful service over the years. There are a few stations in the great metropolitan centres that do not seem to perform a service that appeals very much to many of us in this house, but I suppose they must be performing some kind of service or the people would not pay for the advertising. The stations in the smaller places, catering to local needs, supporting local causes and giving a greater sense of community to those localities, have proven to be a very valuable addition to our Canadian patrimony.
I, for my part, feel that anything we do which would have the effect of weakening the detached and independent character of these stations would be most unfortunate. I have never favoured the idea of having them linked up in great chains, although economies might be effected in some ways by having local networks for limited purposes. I feel, however, that the greater the independence of the

private stations and the greater the local character they can have, the better. I do believe that every Canadian today who has given any serious, detached and objective thought to this matter-even the most ardent socialists-now feels this way or at any rate so express themselves.
There is no doubt that there is a problem, although I have always thought it was rather more psychological than really practical. With respect to the situation between the private stations and the C.B.C., a psychological situation has been created in the last few years supported by very respectable organizations and very respectable arguments, arguments which, on the face of them, appeal at first blush to any liberal minded person. These arguments are to the effect that there is something wrong about the regulation of these private stations by the operating officials of the public service. This was one, although I do not think by any means the most important, of the problems which were submitted to the Fowler commission, and I thought that commission had suggested the happiest possible solution of that problem. I agree that there was a genuine grievance on the part of the private stations with respect to the actual operating personnel of the C.B.C. carrying out this regulatory function as opposed to the board of governors. I believe it is a good thing to have individual C.B.C. stations competing with private stations for listeners. I see nothing wrong with that, in fact I think it is a very good thing but, at the same time, we did not wish to see a situation created wherein there would be two systems in this country; we wanted only one, and we, in our party, have always taken that view.
Of course that is not the view which was taken by hon. gentlemen opposite, or some of them, when they sat over here and I exempt the Minister of National Revenue from that charge. I just looked at the record at random this afternoon

because one does not have much time these days to do any continuous research-and when the hon. gentlemen who were then sitting on this side of the house were trying, very ineffectually, to reply to one of the most brilliant speeches made in this house, namely a speech made the previous day on this subject by the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier), who was then the member for Stormont and the minister of transport. I found, as one would expect to find, that the clearest and most precise statement on the position of the Tory party was made by the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton), who was then the private member for Kamloops. I think, in view of what we have in this bill it is perhaps fitting

that I should now place on record what the member for Kamloops had to say at page 3040 of Hansard for March 17, 1953, which reads as follows:
The system we want to see is a parallel system to that which prevails in our railway communications, which are still governed by the national policy laid down by a Conservative government-
These departures from history I will just ignore as I go along.
-and to which the Minister of Transport today paid tribute. We want to see the same system as prevails in air transport, to which the Minister of Transport also paid tribute.
The hon. member did not quite have the gall to suggest that that was also done by a Conservative government.
We want to see that policy prevail in the field of television broadcasting particularly, because we believe that policy would preserve the right of parliament through the regulatory body to lay down conditions and regulations under which television programs might be presented, and to prescribe the Canadian content of the programs. These stations would, nevertheless, be allowed freedom of operation and competition within those limits, under a policy which would serve the interests of the Canadian people with respect to building up a television system, and consistent with the building up of Canadian talent and Canadian programs, but without the dead hand which is now holding back that development as is the case under the misguided government television policy.
That is what the Minister of Justice had to say when he was on this side of the house; but the Minister of National Revenue took a rather different view of what we had done when he spoke in this house on June 3 of this year, and I feel I should recall to hon. members the words used by that minister as recorded at page 812 of Hansard for that date:
This year, under the aegis of this government-*
That is to say the government of which he is a member.
-I am not speaking politically now at all because other governments gave the C.B.C. financial support, too-

speechtext: We did a good job with it.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext:
You did a good job with it; there is no question about that, but we are going to do a better one with it.
It was precisely those words used by the Minister of National Revenue, more than anything else said during this session, that lulled some of us on this side of the house into what I can only now describe as a false sense of security, and of course we were the more disillusioned when we saw what it was that the Minister of National Revenue, whose heart was shown to be in the right place last June, had been compelled by the exigencies of cabinet solidarity to accept in late August.
Broadcasting
I am sure that all of us feel that the minister must have tried to put up a very strong rearguard action because, after all, it took him from June 3-which would have been approximately a reasonable date at which to bring in this legislation if any consideration was given to parliament or to the rights of parliament instead of taking until I believe a week ago today, August 18, to get his colleagues to go even one-quarter of the way. I say, like the Leader of the Opposition, that one-quarter of the way is just not good enough. We are far better off with the law as it is than we would be if this bill were passed, far better off.
If there were any hope of defeating the bill of course that would be the best thing to do with it. We could then start all over again, but of course the government can prevent that. It does, however, seem to me that the government might have a sober second thought as a result of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Dollard and might consider whether it should not accept his amendment and allow this matter to rest. While the government was itself resting a little during the recess, it could give the matter some further consideration and could also allow the rest of us to give some further consideration to this very important problem, because this bill does attempt to alter fundamentally the whole structure of broadcasting in Canada. We had hoped it was going to be altered for the better, along the lines of the report of the Fowler commission. I do not accept, and I do not think anyone accepts, that report in its entirety but, speaking generally, I do feel it is the most useful guide we could have at the present time to legislation of this nature.
In order to illustrate a little further how widely and how fundamentally this bill does differ from what the Fowler commission recommended, I should like, as the Leader of the Opposition did, to read one or two passages from the report and I do not wish to trespass on the time of the house by repeating the reading of any of those parts which were read by the Leader of the Opposition. I should like to read, first of all, from the chapter entitled "The regulation of broadcasting", on page 90, beginning at the last paragraph:
We think there have in fact been two public elements involved in radio and television broadcasting. This factual separation of powers should be more precisely defined in law. One of these elements should be an operating agency, engaged in the operation of publicly owned stations and national networks and in the production and distribution of a national program service throughout Canada. We think that the phrase "national program serviGe" should, if possible, have a more detailed definition as to its geographical scope and intended purpose than has been given up to the

present time. If this agency is given precise responsibilities it should also be given powers sufficient to discharge those responsibilities, and financial resources, on an assured basis, adequate to do the job that parliament intends it to do. A crown company seems to be the simplest and most familiar form for this agency to take. The existing Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, with minor changes in its statutory powers and organization, can be this agency. Many of the subsequent chapters of this report will deal in detail with the powers, organization, operation and finances of the C.B.C.
The other public agency in the Canadian broadcasting field should be a board created and authorized to act for parliament, and responsible to parliament, for the direction and supervision of the Canadian Broadcasting system. This board should have responsibility for all elements in Canadian broadcasting. It should not, we suggest, be part of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and its members should not, as in the present statute, comprise the corporation. The provision in section 3 of the Broadcasting Act of 1936, whereby the corporation is made to consist of the board of 11 governors was no doubt a familiar form of statutory provision and a natural method of applying the concepts of private company law to a crown corporation. In other crown companies it may not matter, but in broadcasting it has probably contributed to some public confusion as to the nature of relations between the governing board and the operating corporation.

-the suggested changes are made, it is to be hoped that this long and frequently bitter argument about a separate regulatory body will come to an end, and private broadcasters will accept their true role as valued and essential partners with the C.B.C. in the single Canadian broadcasting system.
As compared with those recommendations, what in fact have we here? When I read the bill first, sitting here in my place after it was distributed, I turned to someone sitting beside me and said: "This bill reminds me of nothing so much as the Austro-Hungarian empire before 1914; there is an uneasy kind of duality; no one knows where any of the responsibility lies; it is an utterly

ramshackle structure which is almost certain to fall to pieces if it does not result in some kind of civil war."
It is obvious that you cannot have any clarity with diffused responsibilities. Our great pride in our system of government as compared with any other rests on the fact that the line of responsibility under our system is clear-you always know who to blame and where the blame should rest. It seems to me that it is not desirable to get into this mixed system where nobody is to blame and where nobody has clear responsibility. Who is going to govern the C.B.C. if this bill is adopted; the board of broadcast governors, as Fowler recommended; or this board of directors which has been conjured up like a rabbit out of a hat; or the minister to whom the board of directors of the C.B.C. would be responsible, and responsible in a fashion that I never expected to find in any broadcasting legislation?
I am surprised at the minister framing legislation containing such a phrase as "during pleasure for seven years". I do not know who invented that phrase. I am not a lawyer, and I may never become one, but I have read a lot of statutes in my time. It may be that the minister can produce some precedents for this, and it may be that some of those precedents might apparently prove embarrassing, but I must say that if there are precedents they are probably bad precedents. You either are there during pleasure or you are there during a term of years. It seems to me it is a plain contradiction in terms. A term of years during good behaviour is included in the provision respecting the board of broadcast governors. That is an understandable, normal provision. There is also a normal provision for the determination by some one of what is good behaviour. I do not know if the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Smith) has been giving consideration to this matter but I would be rather interested to hear his views on the phrase, "during pleasure for seven years."
The only construction I could put upon it is that they can stay there for seven years if they keep on pleasing the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) for seven years and that is precisely the thing of which we were afraid. That is precisely what we were afraid of, as I said at the committee stage on the resolution, when the minister hinted to us that the government was not following any of the recommendations of the Fowler commission about the financing of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. At that time I believe I used the phrase they would have to go on bended knee to the Minister of Finance but, unless the Minister of Finance
Broadcasting
is to be the minister responsible, it looks to me as though they will have to bend one knee to the Minister of Finance and one knee to some other minister and try to please them both. That may be possible. It may be there is such harmony in the cabinet that if you please one minister you please them all but perhaps one may be permitted to be a trifle sceptical about the clear lines of responsibility about which I was speaking a few moments ago in a situation like that.
It seems to me there should be no one whatever in the new C.B.C. set-up reporting to a minister. If we are to follow the broad scheme that the Minister of National Revenue is asking us to follow in his bill, the C.B.C. should report to the board of broadcast governors in exactly the same way as the management of the C.B.C. in the past and up to the present has reported to the board of governors of the C.B.C. and the government's relations and parliament's relations should be with the board of governors and with no one else.
Here we are going to have a situation, as was pointed out by my friend the hon. member for Dollard, where we will have the board of broadcast governors perhaps reporting to one minister, and the C.B.C. reporting to another, and in addition the C.B.C. having to go to the Minister of Finance for its funds. It is a preposterous kind of arrangement. As the Leader of the Opposition so very well pointed out this morning, it is just inconceivable that it could ever work.
What is even more serious, in my view, is that it opens the door wide to political interference. Here you have the president and the vice president of this great broadcasting organization appointed during pleasure. They can be fired at any time without explanation by the governor in council. They are the people who will be in charge of the operations of the corporation and they will be reporting to a minister. In some vague way they also have over them this entity, the board of broadcast governors. Where are the lines of responsibility going to be drawn? There is no clarity and there is no certainty but there is every opportunity and every incentive-and one would have to be almost more than human to resist the pressure that there is bound to be-for political interference. I suggested the other day and I still think it is true that perhaps the government would not be so crude as to threaten to cut down the appropriation if they did not behave. But the carrot will often accomplish much more than the stick, as we well know.

It is certainly something I would have thought would not lend itself to any degree to five year plans. But what seems to me is very essential is that by one device or another the C.B.C. should have a certainty as to a minimum amount of revenue. For my own part I again express the feeling that they also should have a certainty as to a maximum, because I do believe the methods of financing of the C.B.C. up to now-and here I agree with what the Minister of National Revenue said earlier this session-are no longer satisfactory. Indeed, I doubt if they have ever been completely satisfactory or if the problem was ever wholly solved, and that is the principal reason why Mr. St. Laurent and Mr. Harris asked their colleagues to join with them in recommending to His Excellency that this royal commission be set up. It was precisely to solve this problem in a more satisfactory way.
In order to have political independence of the government it is essential that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation should have a certain minimum income, but equally, in order to protect the treasury, which is a consideration of which we must never lose sight, there should also be a maximum, in my view. Since the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is not subject to those commercial pressures which commercial operators have to meet- that is to say their balance sheet-and because, of course, it does not have the same kind of objective measures of service that the railways and organizations of that kind have, it seems to me that by imposing a

maximum you do enforce economy upon the organization. There may be three or four things they would like to do, all of which would be desirable, but there will not be enough money to do them all, and they must make a choice among them and cut their coat according to their cloth. I believe that is a good thing for any public agency. An ordinary government department is financially controlled through the treasury board and other devices and also through the annual appropriations in parliament. But, as I say, annual appropriations are most undesirable in this case for two reasons; first, because there would be a lack of the certainty needed to give the corporation independence and, second, because it would open the door wide to political interference or the suspicion of political interference.
I am not making any accusation to the effect that there is any member of the government who presently has any such design. I am not saying that at all. Perhaps I would not have complete confidence in all of them but I am not making any such suggestion. I do say, however, that insensibly these things can happen, if the opportunity is there, and it is our duty as a parliament not to have the opportunity there. It is not necessary and it is not desirable.
It seems to me that what is necessary and desirable is that there should be a period of years long enough to provide a reasonable degree of stability or, if possible, some mechanical formula such as the formula-I just give it by way of illustration-for calculating university grants, where again we have been very anxious in this parliament to make it abundantly clear that there was no interference with provincial rights; some mechanical formula depending on the growth of the population and the value of money, or something of that kind, something which could not be changed at the whim of the Minister of Finance or of the governor in council, to determine what these C.B.C. revenues should be.
It does seem to me that what is suggested here is wholly and utterly unsatisfactory. It is made worse by this provision that the operating agency, the C.B.C., should be responsible in some respects, which are not defined, to the board of broadcast governors and in other respects, which are also not defined, to a minister, and that the operating heads of the C.B.C., the two chief executive officers, should be employed during pleasure. That, sir, is something which I hope the government, if they persist with this bill, which I sincerely hope they will not, will take out of the bill in committee.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext: Is it not true that over the years, until very recently, those loans to the C.B.C. have all been repaid?

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext:
I have not the balance sheets here, but I do not think so. The Fowler commission recommended they be wiped out. As they said, it was a foolish thing to be getting money from the government with one hand and paying back the interest on these loans with another. I have not the figures in front of me, but I think the hon. member will find that the amounts are still very substantial. If they were repaid, then they were paid back with moneys parliament voted; that is about the size of it. I say, therefore, that at least since 1954, there was a grant voted of $6,500,000 by parliament to be paid in three years, and even before that parliament granted moneys to the C.B.C. In 1957 there was $18,250,000 granted in addition to the revenue from the excise tax. In 1958, on the estimates the hon. gentlemen opposite prepared and tabled in this house before their government went out, there was an annual grant of $24,343,000 submitted to parliament. There is, therefore, absolutely nothing new in this situation of getting money from parliament. It is true that from a philosophical or theoretical point of view a good argument could be made out that they should have their own funds. It would be a good thing if the C.B.C. did not have to get any money from parliament at all.
However, this party believes in the supremacy of parliament, and I think the country generally does. I think hon. gentlemen opposite expect, when you are dealing with moneys to the extent that we are here today, then it is time that parliament expressed its judgment on that. Parliament would do that anyway. There is no possibility in the world of dealing with $40 million or $50 million and avoiding a discussion on it, even if any government wanted to avoid a discussion on it which I do not think any government would. This bill faces that situation realistically and says that the C.B.C. shall come to parliament for annual grants.

Look at the sections of the old act, and what do you find? You find the same provisions exactly. Section 17 says that the governor in council may authorize certain things and provide money for them on application. Then section 18 says that the corporation shall deal with the Minister of Finance. All of these sections here refer to the governor in council and refer to the Minister of Finance. What is the situation with respect to the C.B.C. now? It cannot get more than $25,000 without going, cap in hand, as my friends say, to the minister who, at the moment, happens to be me, and have the minister recommend to the cabinet this expenditure of $25,000, whether it is for a radio tower or for a program.
You will notice that nothing has been said about one important aspect of the bill, Mr. Speaker. We have heard a lot of talk about this terrible thing which is being done to the C.B.C., threatening its integrity, and so on. That is sheer nonsense. I have not heard a word today about the fact that under this measure the C.B.C. can spend up to $100,000 without going to the minister. We increased this ceiling largely because electronic equipment is so expensive today that when you are in the realm of $25,000 you are only buying relatively cheap material.
There is another thing in that section which has not been mentioned in this debate today, and that is that this limitation of $100,000 has no reference whatever to programming. Under the present act, which I am administering today, the C.B.C. has to come to me, and through me to cabinet, for approval to spend $25,000 on a program. There are very few programs today that do not cost more than $25,000. Under the bill which we have introduced, and which I am asking this house to pass, there is no limitation whatever on programming. A criticism could be made that there is a danger of the C.B.C. overspending; I prefer to deal with that criticism rather than be open to the other one. Now, and in the future, the C.B.C. can spend money for programs, program material and anything necessary in connection with programs, without any limitation whatever in so far as the government is concerned but subject, of course, to living within the general financial framework within which it has to operate. If that is not a substantial improvement over the existing system, I should like to know what is. Amidst all these dire forebodings and rumblings of doom I should have liked to have heard some discussion of those things which have been done for the C.B.C.
I do not believe it is essential or advisable that I should take up much more time. There

is, of course, one other matter which is very imnortant and that is the section providing for the five-year program. The Leader of the Opposition said he did not think that would be very effective. I feel it is, at least, a distinct step in the right direction. I think it is something that will be effective. It is true there is nothing in there that says it shall be binding; it does not have to be submitted to parliament. However, I am sure if the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate gets up at the opening of the session and asks for the provision of the budget, I do not see how it could be denied, and I do not think it should be.

It is a five-year program. The hon. member for Port Arthur said he thought it should be a longer one, and it might be. You cannot chop off a five-year item just like that. In general, it gives a picture of the capital commitments for the next five years. The C.B.C. has the commitment of the government, at any rate, that these moneys will be provided and, subject to some unforeseen disaster such as a change of government which is something that would be an unmitigated disaster, there can be no question but that the C.B.C. knows they have this capital framework within which they may operate. They need to come to parliament for current operations. It is true that Fowler recommended the reverse. However, he said he only used the capital item as something for which they had to go to parliament in order to give parliament an opportunity for discussion. If hon. gentlemen get involved in a discussion of programs they may be called out of order by the Speaker, but in any discussion of capital, such as recommended by Fowler, there is no hon. gentleman who would not be able to carry on a discussion in a very wide field. It is immaterial, so far as I can see, and so far as the discussion is concerned, whether the discussion takes place on a capital item or current operations.
Something has been said about the two boards getting in each other's hair-I think that was the expression used by the Leader of the Opposition. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate quoted at some length from Fowler in connection with this matter who pointed out that two boards were not necessary. If one looks at page 135 of the Fowler report, one finds that he was referring to two boards of similar personnel involved in the regulation of broadcasting. This bill was designed so that regulation will be carried out by the board of broadcast governors and the financial and other administration of 57071-3-258

the C.B.C. as an operating unit will be carried on by the board of directors of the C.B.C. It is true that you may get a conflict. I know what has been said about one strong one and one weak one, or something of that kind, but I doubt if that follows. There are two different views but the board of broadcast governors is the overriding agency which is going to lay down the regulations and to enforce them, I hope and believe, and under which regulations all operations will be carried out in the future. The board of directors will administer the C.B.C. as the business and operating unit. There is no thought whatsoever of destroying the single system, or anything of that kind.
This, I believe, is going to make it better for the private broadcasting stations in that they can go to an independent body. Some of the criticisms levelled at the C.B.C. were probably not justified but the psychological problem is there. The fact that the private broadcaster had to go to the C.B.C., which was operating networks and perhaps operating a competing station in some communities to make application to the C.B.C., caused frictions and difficulties and I believe inter-ferred with the efficiency and the public relations of the C.B.C. to a marked extent.
I am confident that when this bill is passed, the C.B.C. will find itself in a stronger position than ever before because that criticism will be removed, and it will be able to carry on as an operating unit and an absolutely independent body will administer the applications and will deal with these matters from both a public and private point of view. I believe that when the bill goes through and becomes law it will be found that we have solved this fundamental problem which has bedevilled broadcasting for 15 years because of the ambiguity of the situation and the criticisms in connection with it. This government has tried to clear up this problem and I believe we have succeeded in doing so. The future of broadcasting will, as I say, depend upon the personnel of the board of broadcast governors but I am confident that men and women will be found in this country who will man those positions and will give good administration to Canadian broadcasting in the future, making it even stronger and better than it has been in the past.
Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the
Opposition): Mr. Speaker, I have no apology to make for the fact that I am taking advantage of the amendment moved in order to say a few words-and they will only be a few words-on this bill for the second time. After all, we have been debating this matter only since 11.30 this morning and we are now perhaps on the point of voting on
