second reading at five o'clock this afternoon. As has been pointed out by more than one speaker, we are dealing with a matter of the most fundamental importance and I would have hoped that in view of that fact we would have heard some statements about this bill, its purposes, objectives and principles, from members opposite.
Although it may be arguable, broadcasting is now perhaps the most important agency for the formation of public opinion and the dissemination of information which exists. Whether this is true or not, no one can deny that there can hardly be anything more important in a democratic society than broadcasting by radio and television. We in Canada know-although perhaps not so definitely or so tragically as is known in some other countries -what can happen to public opinion and what can happen to a country if this agency gets into the wrong hands or goes the wrong way. I am not suggesting that anything like that is going to happen in Canada; of course it is not. But this is a special problem for us in another respect because there is perhaps no country in the world where its own broadcasting agency can be more influenced or where its public opinion can be more influenced by the operations in this field of a neighbouring and friendly country. Therefore we have a duty to ourselves and to this parliament fully to discuss the principles of this bill in the light of that important fact.
While the debate on second reading may be coming to a close, we hope to have an opportunity to go through this bill in committee, section by section, and at that time to be able to point out to the minister the significance of some of these provisions as we see them and the way in which they do differ from the recommendations made by a royal commission set up to deal with this matter; a royal commission which did deal with it very effectively and in great detail and has made its report. If we keep on referring to that royal commission and to its report it is because the impression has been created that this bill is based on the report of the Fowler commission; I think it has already been made clear, although perhaps we can make it even clearer in our discussions in committee, that there are some very important differences between the provisions of this bill and the recommendations of that committee.
The minister has said that we really have not pointed out very many weaknesses in the bill; that we on this side of the house have expressed forebodings which no doubt will be removed after we have had some experience of the working of this bill if it is passed. I will leave it to the record to
[Mr. Pearson.!
indicate whether we have or have not pointed out specific and concrete weaknesses in the bill as we see them; I believe some of the arguments we have advanced against it have not been met by the minister although, as I say, we will perhaps have a chance to deal with those matters in committee. So far as our forebodings are concerned-and like other speakers I do not include the minister in this particular foreboding-I particularly have in mind the views expressed by some hon. members opposite in years gone by as to the functions of the government in respect of broadcasting. These forebodings have been increased by the fact that we are discussing this bill in the house, not in June when it could have been sent to a committee, but on August 25, at the end of this session.
I will just take a moment, Mr. Speaker, to itemize the more important criticisms we have already made. We do feel that this bill could weaken the national system of broadcasting and could make it possible- although I am not going any further than that because I want to be fair and we do not know exactly how this bill is going to work out-its provisions do make it easier than was previously the case to develop two systems of broadcasting. As I have said, I did not appear to leave any concrete impression in his mind, but I hope perhaps to do so and to raise some forebodings even in that mind when we go through this bill section by section in committee. I hope we will have a chance to deal with the details at that time.
However, section 10 of the bill does state formally-and this is the governing section of this bill-the objects and purposes of this board of broadcasting governors as appointed. But there is no reference in that section to the maintenance or strengthening of the national system or to the paramount

importance of the public service aspect as the purpose of broadcasting. I do not mean to say that this could not be developed as the bill operates, but some of these forebodings about which we have been talking do arise out of the fact that no mention is made in this section, indeed no mention is made in any part of the bill, of this matter, this purpose. Yet, if one reads the Fowler report, as the minister must have more than once, one will see that in practically every chapter of that report the commissioners stressed the vital importance of one national system of broadcasting, primarily carried on as a public service.
My second criticism, which the minister says is not justified, is that this bill seems not to strengthen but to weaken the position of the C.B.C. Perhaps we will also be able to establish that point a little more clearly when we deal with the detailed provisions of the bill. Surely the fact that we now have two boards of a comparable character, two boards reporting to the govermnent, two boards reporting to parliament through the same minister or two different ministers; surely the fact that two boards have to make two reports through two ministers does emphasize that there has in some way been created a division of responsibility and, perhaps, a division of broadcasting. I cannot, myself, believe that this kind of division in the channel, in the line of responsibility is not going to have a bad effect on the C.B.C. It runs absolutely against the report of the Fowler commission. Were I to read page 135 and following paragraphs of the report I think I could prove to the hon. gentleman that that is true, and that the Fowler commission did not recommend this kind of relationship between the regulatory board and the C.B.C.
One other specific criticism is directed against the cumbersome nature of the organization. We cannot for one moment accept the minister's statement that this bill will clear up the present situation and clarify confusion and remove, as the minister said a minute or two ago, ambiguity. We think it will have the opposite effect, especially when the two managerial heads of the C.B.C. are to be appointed at pleasure and can, therefore, be removed, if necessary, at pleasure.
The minister explained this by saying the government proposed to appoint them at pleasure because they were managerial personnel of the C.B.C. That is the very reason why they should be given increased protection and increased security. It would have been much less damaging, I think, to the C.B.C. if the other members of the board had been appointed at pleasure.

It is perfectly true that the C.B.C. in the last few years, because of increasing expenditures,-the reasons for which we all understand-in the development of its national broadcasting system has had to go to the government for increased grants. That royal commission found that the C.B.C. had been well run and well administered. After giving as much consideration to this financial aspect of broadcasting as to any other phase, this royal commission made a report.
I do not propose to read this chapter on financing into the record, but I will make a reference to it-pages 274 to page 279-in which it dealt with the provision of operating funds. The commission, in this chapter, emphasizes the importance of giving the C.B.C. some assurance of a continuing income

for this purpose and of giving it as much independence as possible subject to parliamentary control-we all accept that-and an assurance of a certain income over a period of years ahead. The royal commission put forward certain specific plans for that purpose. It also stated that this could be accomplished without any infringement of the right of parliamentary control. Perhaps I should emphasize that again. One way in which the royal commission said that parliamentary control could be insured was by having the corporation go to the house every year, whatever procedure might be in effect with respect of operating expenses, for its capital budget.
This particular bill, Mr. Speaker, as I said this morning and as the minister has admitted this afternoon, is exactly the reverse of that recommendation. The Fowler report says on page 271-this is the reason why they suggested the corporation should go to parliament every year for its capital budget-that there is a practical difficulty with regard to forecasting capital cost over a six-year period.
The report went on to say:
These developments of physical plant and equipment of a publicly owned broadcasting enterprise ought to be considered by the government and parliament at regular and frequent intervals. These are the things that really determine the course of future activities. This is where the policy can be effectively determined rather than in the sporadic examination of programs or other operating details. This is the surest way, we believe, to carry out the intent that the broadcasting system should be directly subject to parliamentary control and supervision.
That particular recommendation of the committee was not accepted. But now the corporation must go to parliament every year for an appropriation for all its operating expenses. We continue to believe that the recommendation of the Fowler commission in regard to financing will be more effective, will not impair parliamentary control in any way but will be more efficient with respect to the future conduct of broadcasting in Canada. I do not think the minister should dismiss these differences between us in respect of this bill as a small matter. They seem to us to be almost fundamental-the fact that the C.B.C. is to go to parliament for all its income, except that which it derives from commercial sources, every year; the fact that the president and the vice president are to be appointed, not on the recommendation of the board but directly by the government; the fact that they would hold office at pleasure for seven years; and the fact that the board of the C.B.C. reports directly through a minister to the government and not through a regulatory board. - '

Surely I have said enough to indicate that there are important differences of opinion between us and those who drew up this bill. We continue, notwithstanding what the minister has said, to hold the view that this bill if it becomes law will not advance the cause of national broadcasting in this country, will not strengthen public control of national broadcasting and will not emphasize, as it should be emphasized, that broadcasting is a national service for national development. We believe, on the other hand, that this bill will leave broadcasting in Canada in a weaker position, from the public point of view-and that is of paramount importance-than it was before it was introduced.

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of my associates in this group I feel I should explain why we are going to vote with the government against the amendment brought in by the Liberal party. Perhaps the most important factor-and at first glance it appears to be a short range one-is that a six-month hoist coming at this time when we so badly need regulations will be far too damaging to a situation that is very nebulous. We in this group believe that this would open up just another six or eight months of propaganda and warfare especially on the part of the agencies we fear the most in their efforts to hamstring the national broadcasting setup, and I refer generally to the C.A.R.T.B. and the private broadcasters. It seems to me tins would do nothing more than play into the hands of these people.
Our misgivings about the bill have by no means been completely allayed by the minister's statement. We would still very much like to have a statement on the bill and on the government's intention from the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker). That may go begging, but we would still very much like to have that statement.
Everything depends on the board of broadcast governors; but who has the choice of picking the board? There is almost an innocence in the reliance of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) on the appointment of the board: wait until the board is selected; everything will depend on it; instructions cannot be given to the board; detailed policy cannot be threshed out because that would restrain the board. But who is going to appoint the board? I believe we all have a good idea who will be the key person appointing that board and he is now sitting in the front benches on the government side of the house. We would all like to hear some words from him as to the direction the board might go. What is the kind of person

he feels should be chosen for the board? That is one of many questions to which we would like to have an answer.
Clause 10 of the bill has been read into the record four or five times today and it does sound pretty good. It is rather difficult to quarrel with it. However, it is not as detailed or specific as the draft bill contained in the report of the Fowler commission. That is why so much is going to be left in an uncertain condition. If the bill goes through without any more detail I can anticipate that we are going to have a dandy guessing game for the next several months. Everyone will be speculating; it will all depend on whom the government appoints; whom does the Prime Minister have in mind; who has been visiting his office lately; thus the speculation will grow.
I wish the government would go a little further in stipulating the kind of things it wants the board of broadcast governors to do. I cannot believe that the government by its choice of personnel is not going to influence the direction of future policy of broadcasting in Canada. That is why we will continue to have our misgivings about this.
The minister indicated earlier that he was giving a complete assurance that a committee on broadcasting would be established at the next session of the house. I should like to put a question to the minister at this time. Will the minister give us his complete assurance now that at the next session of the house a committee will be established and have before it the three permanent members of the board of broadcast governors so an opportunity will be provided to question them as well as anyone else attached to radio including people in the C.B.C. in order to see what the status is early in 1959?

Mr. Speaker, when the minister introduced the resolution on which the bill is based a few days ago he was reported by the press as having said that the bill brought about only one major change. To some extent that is correct, but I think that most of us are concerned about the many other changes which will flow from this major change of setting up a separate regulatory body. Radio and broadcast policies have been well established by parliament down through the years and

Broadcasting
they were summarized in the committee report of 1942-43. Perhaps it would be worth while to put on record in this debate the findings of that committee. In its report on Canadian broadcasting made during the session of 1942-43 the committee had this to say:
Your committee would like to preface its recommendations by stating its confidence in the framework provided by the Canadian Broadcasting Act, 1936. In the reports as well as in debates in parliament, a number of principles governing national broadcasting in Canada were enunciated and emphasized. Your committee now desires to reaffirm these principles as stated in the reports of the committees for the years mentioned in brackets:
(a)	The paramount importance of a single national authority to control all broadcasting in the public interest: (1932).
(b)	The public ownership of all high powered stations under a national system of broadcasting, with low power stations individually operated or co-ordinated in relation to the dominant system; (1932).
(c)	The co-ordination of all broadcasting in Canada through exclusive control being vested in the nationally-owned system of:
(i)	The character of all programs, political or otherwise, broadcast by all stations and of the advertising content thereof; and
(ii)	All wireline networks used for carrying broadcast programs; (1936).
(d)	The independence and flexibility of administration of the national broadcasting authority to be assured by its constitution as a public corporation. Under this constitution decisions as to policy are to be made by its board of governors while administration is to be unified under a general manager, and an assistant general manager, responsible to the board for the conduct of all business of the corporation;-

Mr. Speaker, the summary of all these principles amounted to a partnership between the national system and the private system, each to be operated and managed in such a way as to complement each other in the public interest. The reason I put these principles on the record is to show that the present bill departs from principles which have been established all through the years and have been approved by every parliament

and every committee since 1932. The bill destroys that concept of partnership completely because under the bill the private stations and networks will no longer be junior partners in a single system but will be competitors. They have been made competitors under the bill and both the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, the public system, and the private system are now to be under the control of another body.
That brings up another question as to the exact status of the public system under the new set-up. In the past the C.B.C. has been completely responsible to its board of governors and that board of governors in turn has been responsible to parliament. Now we have a divided authority because the public system will be responsible to this supra-body that is being set up and also to parliament. I think that is a matter of concern because the public system can certainly no longer function with the freedom that it did before.
I should like to say here that we in Newfoundland are very fortunate with respect to our private stations. I think they are second to none in any part of Canada. I would say that they are a splendid example of the private system and the public system complementing each other. I should like to take a moment to pay tribute to the extent to which these private stations go in developing local talent. This is particularly true of station CJON, which has developed a glee club and put on local plays. This station carries many live programs, on both radio and television, which provide a fine op-, portunity for the development of our local talent. The C.B.C. has done its share, too, in this regard. We have had plays performed written by our own Ted Russell, one of our prominent Newfoundland playwrights, who is making quite a name for himself. A couple of Sundays ago we heard a program which was devoted to Newfoundland folklore. I hope I can get a copy of what Uncle Mose said on that occasion because I want to read it to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) and the Postmaster General (Mr. Hamilton) so they will know what Uncle Mose had to say about the post office and the Canadian National Telegraphs in Newfoundland. I hope I can get that before the minister's estimates come before the house.
I believe this is a perfect example of the two systems complementing each other, but we are doing away with that under this bill. There will not be the same compulsion now to complement each other. Under the previous system the private stations had no rights of their own, and that was understandable because the airwaves are limited. They are part of the public domain and no

single person could have any vested right in them. Consequently they must be allocated year after year by the state. Under this bill, the private stations have acquired rights which they did not have before. They now find themselves on an equal footing with the public system. It does not take a great deal of imagination to see that this is not going to work out. I think a system of partnership is ideally suited to conditions in Canada, in our present stage of development. I believe that in 50 or 80 years time, whatever it is, when we have doubled our population and when we do not have as many sparsely populated localities as we have today, there will be a necessity for a change in our system. However, I cannot visualize any conditions under which a competitive system will be superior to a partnership.
On several occasions I have brought to the attention of this house the needs of my own riding and the fact that those needs are not being met by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation today.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext: I hope the hon. member does not intend to bring those needs to the attention of the house again, as he will be out of order.

speechtext:
No, I will have the opportunity to do that when the estimates are before the house. What I do want to point out is that the gap in the coverage which cannot be filled by the public system is being filled by the private system. If we alter this setup now the situation must develop, as our leader explained this afternoon, whereby a private station must of necessity become interested in profit because without profit it cannot operate. These stations, therefore, must be interested in those localities which have the densest population and the best market. I do not see how anybody could administer fairly on a basis that will, on the one hand, give the private station a market in which to make sufficient profit to make their operation worthwhile, and at the same time give the public system a chance to earn its way so that it will not be such a severe drain on our taxpayers.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, that even yet the government will take another look at this bill and not force it through the house at this time, but withdraw it and let everybody have an opportunity to see what is in it, formulate their ideas and then at the next session of parliament set up a committee so that all those ideas could be heard. This procedure, I am sure, would result in a much better bill than we have at the present time.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was not very happy about this bill when I spoke this afternoon on the amendment and appealed to the government to put off this legislation and to take a sober second look at it. I very much regret that the government did not see fit to adopt the motion which would have made that possible.
As the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) has said, in the circumstances we on this side of the house have no alternative but to vote against the measure, and I must say that the minister's defence of the measure made me all the more convinced that this was the right and proper course to take.
The minister made a statement which I cannot allow to go unchallenged. The Leader of the Opposition referred to it, but said he would spare the house quotations from the Fowler report on this point. I am afraid that being less forbearing than the Leader of the Opposition I do not intend to do so. I am not going to quote at length what the Leader of the Opposition quoted earlier today, but I am going to read one or two short sentences which seem to me to demonstrate completely the fallacy of the statement made by the minister. Indeed, I would say that if the minister did not comprehend this part of the Fowler report any better than he seems to have done the others, then it is perhaps not surprising that the rest of the bill bears so little relation to what is recommended in that report.
The minister stated-and if I am not stating his position absolutely correctly I would be very happy to be interrupted and corrected -that this bill was doing precisely what the Fowler commission had recommended, namely setting up a separate regulatory body. The Fowler commission recommended nothing of the kind, and in fact it condemned in the most specific and categorical language the establishment of a separate regulatory board. I read the first sentences on page 134 of the report as follows:
The real objection to the proposal for a "separate regulatory board" is a practical one. It is likely to prove unworkable and is certain to be cumbersome and inefficient.
In other words, the Fowler commission in the most categorical language, using the very

Broadcasting
words used by the minister, recommended against and not for a separate regulatory board. Again, at the bottom of that page and at the top of page 135, appear these words:
As a practical matter, we do not believe you can have two administrative bodies, appointed by the same government and with similar personnel involved in the regulation of broadcasting, without having duplication of expense and effort, undesirable friction between the two, and a loss of efficiency.
It seems to me that that disposes of the minister's claim in regard to what he, I think, described as the fundamental recommendation of the commission being followed by the government. The government has moved in a direction diametrically opposed to the recommendation of the commission, but this fact is at least camouflaged by the use of the language employed by the Fowler commission. The board which the government proposes to set up is described as a board of broadcast governors but it is quite clear that this board of broadcast governors is not going to have exclusive jurisdiction over broadcasting and that is, as I said earlier and as I repeat now, one of the fundamental objections, though perhaps not the most serious one, that we have to this bill.
I think the Leader of the Opposition was not just fearing something intangible when he talked about the dangers in this legislation with respect to our arriving at two different and perhaps competing and conflicting broadcasting systems in this country, and I call as a witness to the fact that this is not a purely theoretical danger the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming). The Minister of Finance when he sat on this side of the house was an expert on many things, but on no subject did he pontificate more frequently or with greater apparent authority than on the subject of broadcasting. I have before me Hansard for June 4, 1954 and at page 5521 the estimates of the then minister of national revenue were being discussed and the present Minister of Finance had this to say about the C.B.C.:
But the fact of the matter is that as long as it is government policy to attempt to confine people to one source in this rapidly developing means of communication, television, the effects and influence of which on the minds and lives of people are simply incalculable, we are courting a danger to the very fundamentals of our whole conception of freedom.
Hon. members will note that the minister was talking about freedom, and he continues:
I do urge upon the house that the house address itself to the imminent, pressing perils for Canadians of a policy of monopoly which this government has deliberately followed, has deliberately fostered and to which it still unrepentantly adheres. This policy must be put aside. The government must
[Mr. Pickersgill.l
cease to impose monopoly upon the people. Encouragement should be given, with all the safeguards that are available under law, to permitting people to have alternative sources of communication in this important and rapidly expanding field. The time has come, Mr. Chairman, for a drastic change in our policy in relation to regulation in this field.
And I think that is, of course, what the Minister of Finance thinks he is getting now.
The Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) made a good deal of the fact that, in the last year or two, when we were in office we had been obliged by reason of rising costs, particularly those of television broadcasting, and declining revenue from the excise tax, to make temporary and interim appropriations to the C.B.C. That is true; but those were, if my memory correctly serves me, the only appropriations of that character which were made. In all previous cases the financing of the C.B.C. was done on a basis which did not depend upon annual appropriations, and when these annual appropriations were brought in during the last year or two, the minister of finance of that day and the minister reporting to parliament for the C.B.C. were both very apologetic about having to do this kind of thing. It was primarily for that reason and not to settle the question of a separate regulatory body that Mr. Harris and the former prime minister were so anxious to have a royal commission set up so that this dangerous policy, which we indeed recognized as a dangerous policy-this policy of annual appropriations, which brought the C.B.C. in our opinion too directly under the control of government-could be done away with and something put in its place.
Every device suggested for that purpose was opposed by hon. gentlemen who are now sitting on the treasury benches. I have in my hand Hansard for 1952-53, volume V, and I note that on May 4, 1953, the present Minister of Finance was speaking on the bill to amend the Canadian Broadcasting Act, which was introduced by Mr. Abbott for the purpose of earmarking the excise taxes on radio and television for the use of the C.B.C.
Perhaps some of the newer members will not recall why that was done. It was done because those taxes were fixed at a definite rate; the government could not control the revenue from them, and the C.B.C. got all that was raised from them. It was a period when people were buying television sets in large numbers; a period, also, when great numbers of Canadians could not have television because they were too remote from the broadcasting stations. The government decided -and I think it was a very wise decision -that the people who were getting the benefit of television should, in the main,

pay for it. This was a very neat way of doing it and one which kept control of the C.B.C. out of the government, because this money went automatically to the C.B.C.
The present Minister of Finance took the most violent exception to this proposal, and here is a small part of what he had to say on that occasion. I would not think of inflicting on the house more than a small part of it.
We are expected, as a sovereign parliament, to trust the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to the extent-
Mark those words-"to trust the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation", that is the attitude, that is the state of mind-of the Minister of Finance.
-to the extent that in the one case we make provision in their behalf for a five-year annual grant in advance totalling $312 million.
That is the Massey grant.
Now we are being asked to turn additional revenue over to them without any future control on the part of parliament over it. Why cannot the alternative and sound principle apply, namely that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation trust parliament to make whatever provision is needed year by year in order to meet the known needs of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation?
In other words, bring it under the thumb of the government. The hon. member for Eglin-ton continued:
That is the issue, Mr. Chairman, which is presented by this section and which can be overcome only by an amendment of the type that I have proposed.
Mr. Abbott, who had a great deal of com-monsense and who had an extraordinary capacity for replying to pompous arguments with rather earthy statements, had this to say as recorded on page 4720:
As to this nonsense about having no opportunity to discuss the affairs of the C.B.C.-
I must say that this is very like the language used by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) this afternoon-
As to this nonsense about having no opportunity to discuss the affairs of the C.B.C., may I say I have been in the house for 13 years, and with the possible exception of wheat-
I draw that to the attention of the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue).
-I do not believe any other subject has received such a thorough airing in the house as the affairs of the C.B.C. To use a slang phrase it is pure eyewash to say the House of Commons has not the fullest opportunity to dig into what the C.B.C. is doing and to find out how much money it is spending and to find out how it is spending that money.
We all know that that is perfectly true. We know it is quite unnecessary to have annual appropriations in order to make that true, because there were never any annual appropriations up to the time Mr. Abbott was speaking in 1953. In fact, it has been more 57071-3-259
Broadcasting
true at that time than it has been since the present administration came to office, because although they have made appropriations, up to now they have made those appropriations only by governor general's warrant. Thus there has not been, in the year and two months during which this administration has been in office, much opportunity to consider the finances of the C.B.C.
But there is no doubt that we have the opportunity, and there is no doubt whatsoever that if a scheme of appropriations over a period of years, with minima and maxima set as suggested in various ways by the Fowler commission, for the operating expenses of the C.B.C. there would have to be a bill or a provision in a bill to enable that to be done, and there would be an opportunity at that time of considering it. There would be an annual debate to consider it and, as the Fowler commission very properly suggested, for the capital expenditures, which would be relatively big items about which there might be differences in parliament, there would be annual appropriations and, as the minister very wisely said, if these capital items came before parliament surely some of us would have ingenuity enough to figure out ways for relating arguments on current operations to capital outlays of that sort. If any hon. members should want help as to how to do that I would be willing to offer them a little free advice at any time.
I come back again to this question of financial control. No one on this side of the house is objecting at all to financial control by parliament of the C.B.C. What we are objecting to is financial control by the government of the C.B.C., and that distinction does not yet seem to have penetrated the minds of the occupants of the treasury benches. I will tell the house one reason for our attitude in this regard. The Minister of Finance had something else to say when he was on this side of the house as recently as 1955. I did not get very far in my researches or, no doubt, I would have found a great many more illustrations. But in that year he was talking about the estimates of the Minister of National Revenue. I am only going to quote a little of what he said, but it is very revealing. We all know how flexible the minister is, and how apt to change his mind, but these are his words:
I simply conclude with this. This system, by reason of its developed weaknesses, its inherent unsoundness, its suppression of freedom, its suppression of competition in favour of monopoly and the colossal cost to the Canadian taxpayer, as my colleague, the hon. member for Perth will show, has brought us to the point now in Canada that in this house we are requesting a fundamental revision in policy in relation to radio and television broadcasting.

Broadcasting
So much for the Minister of Finance. I think that before this parliament agrees to make this fundamental change in broadcasting in Canada, a change which affects so intimately the lives of at least 80 per cent of the population of this country, the Minister of Finance, who after all is going to have more control over broadcasting under this set-up than anyone else except the Prime Minister, should come into the house and tell us what his views are and what his feelings are about this matter. It seems to me those quotations I have read give us strong grounds for feeling that to put this corporation and to put the whole broadcasting system of this country at the mercy of the Minister of Finance is not the kind of thing which the Fowler commission had in mind, or the kind of thing which the majority of the people of Canada want.
I said something a moment or two ago about the difference between financial control by parliament and financial control by government. The minister talked almost as though we on this side wanted to prevent debate in this house concerning the C.B.C. We certainly do not. I do not think there is anything healthier than debate about the C.B.C. and I do not see any reason why we should not criticize the C.B.C. in this house if we feel inclined to do so, openly and frankly. What we do not want, and what no person who cares about having a free country wants is to have the ministers in their closets able to control this great agency for the dissemination of objective information. That is what we do not want. It is our duty as a parliament and it is the duty of hon. members in this house not in the government but sitting supporting the government to see that that ideal is upheld.
I appeal at this time, as I used to listen so often to appeals made from this side of the house when I sat on the other side, to the private members in this house to get up and say what they feel about this. Do they feel they want this broadcasting system, the operating part of it, brought under the direct control of the minister administered by two executives who can be fired without notice by the governor in council at any time he pleases? Is that their idea of having an independent broadcasting system in this country?

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext:
It is not mine and I do not believe it is the conception of any person who has any real understanding of freedom, and that, it seems to me, is the fundamental issue here.
So long as we have these annual appropriations, so long as we have these clauses

in this legislation enabling the government to dispense with the executives of this corporation during pleasure, I do not care how pure the government is, human beings being what they are there will be a suspicion. We should not have legislation of that sort. We should remove that suspicion and bring this bill above reproach so these things could not happen.
What is at stake, in my opinion, is one of our essential freedoms. I am not going to transgress the rules of the house but we have been told that before this session ends we are to be asked to consider legislation to guarantee our freedoms. Here is a piece of legislation dealing with one of the fundamental and one of the most important freedoms of all. What do we find? At the present time we have legislation which ensures independence from the government and we are asked to scrap that legislation and substitute for it a measure that will bring the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation under the direct and immediate control of the government in two most objectionable ways. I say that this legislation should not pass and that no one who really cares about freedom should vote for this legislation.
I must say I am not too surprised that this legislation has been introduced. I am a little disappointed that the Minister of National Revenue has been taken in by his colleagues as I believe he has, but I am not too surprised at this legislation.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext: It is the reverse.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext:
Oh no. The minister did rather a good job of attempting to give us the impression that he had put one over on his colleagues, but after we see how closely the bill corresponds with the prognostications of the Minister of Finance it becomes obvious to us who the real author of this bill is, and it is not the Minister of National Revenue.
I have not often been guilty of quoting myself in this house and as a general practice I do not think it is a very laudable one but it did so happen that on October 19 of last year I made a speech in Winnipeg which I am sure no hon. member heard and in it I had something to say about the subject which is now under consideration. I am not going to apologize for repeating now what I said then because I believe it is completely relevant to this measure before the house. What I said on that occasion was that it was a matter of pride to me that after 22 years of Liberal rule one could travel the face of the globe without finding any other country in which the individual has greater freedom than he enjoys in Canada.
I went on to say that this Liberal achievement of freedom for the ordinary citizen-

and it has been a Liberal achievement-is now taken so much for granted in Canada that we have other parties claiming that they are really more liberal than the Liberal party, and we had a demonstration of that, of course, in some of the observations made by the Minister of National Revenue with respect to this bill.

speechtext: Oh yes, Mr. Speaker. As you will see, sir, it is very directly related to it. I will spare you the reading of a paragraph that is not related to it although, since it refers to the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), I am sure that most hon. members on the other side of the house would be very pleased to hear it.

speechtext: Oh no.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext: What I said was that in some of his campaign speeches the Prime Minister deliberately played down the name of his own party and played up his so-called liberalism, and we of the Liberal party can only take that as a compliment. And then I went on to say that the proof of that pudding would be in the eating. I suggested that we Liberals-and I did not mean just the Liberals but all Canadians-had better keep our eyes on what the Prime Minister does without being distracted too much by what he says, and I believe that is very good advice for every one in this country.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext: What about March 31?

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext: To show you that I am not taking too long to come to the subject, I said one of the first places we Liberals had better watch for attacks on freedom was in the field of radio broadcasting. I was censured for making that statement. The Ottawa Journal picked up a report of this address and said there was nothing to this suggestion, that it could never happen; but it is happening right now. I went on to point out that so great has been the freedom of speech and the freedom to criticize in this country that in recent years our national broadcasting system has given more time and more scope to critics of the government than to defenders of the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext: There were a lot more of them.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext:
I said that we as a government never tried to change that and I indicated that 1 made no complaint about that then. But, I said, we Liberals must be vigilant to see that the same freedom to broadcast is maintained under the Tories as 57071-3-259i
Broadcasting
prevailed under a Liberal government and today we see that it is not being done.
I might say, sir, that the next paragraph refers to freedom of trade and gives the same warning. Considering the legislation that is to be called after this bill it will be seen I was not very wide of the mark last October.
There is one respect in which 1 quite agree with the Minister of National Revenue and with the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher). I thought at the resolution stage, as did my leader, that we ought to have this legislation go to a special committee. I thought we ought to call witnesses and give them an opportunity to present their points of view. But, sir, I did not expect this kind of bill. I expected a bill roughly in accord with the recommendations of the Fowler commission. I expected we would have something in the package to resemble the advertisement on the cover but we have something that is entirely and completely different, even in the one respect which the minister called fundamental and with respect to which he said the government had followed the recommendation of the Fowler commission report but which I have shown to be the exact opposite. It seems to me this bill is so far beyond redemption that it would certainly not be practical in the time that any special committee could meet in this session to call the witnesses that would be necessary.
I suppose, in the circumstances, if we cannot persuade the government even at this late stage to stop this folly, to arrest this measure where it is now, to go on to the next item of business and to come back to this next year-this fundamental change, as the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) has said, in one of the most important measures for the national development of this country -we can be outvoted. We know that and we expect we will be. We will do our best in committee to have a few ameliorations to this bill but ameliorations will not make it satisfactory. It is fundamentally wrong in the three respects pointed out by the Leader of the Opposition. It is fundamentally wrong because it has two boards instead of one and thereby threatens to establish two systems instead of one. It is also fundamentally wrong because it brings the corporation directly under the control of a member of the government instead of under the board which always in the past insulated the operating side of radio from direct intervention by the government. In the third place it is wrong because of the financial structure that is suggested.
It seems to me that with legislation of this kind-if the majority insist on putting

Broadcasting
it through-the only thing to do is to take the issue to the eventual arbiters, and I predict that the day will come when this wrong turning will be regretted on the other side of the house as well as on this side, and we shall all want to go back to a system where there is genuine independence and genuine freedom and the guarantee of it in broadcasting.

speakeroldname: Hon. George C. Nowlan (Minister of National Revenue):

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think in deference to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) who has just given an exhibition of histrionics that we would expect from him on this occasion, I at least should pay him the compliment of replying very briefly.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext: If the minister speaks now he will close the debate.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext: The trouble with the former minister, the spokesman of the Liberal party, is that he certainly is disappointed. He is disappointed because, as he pointed out in Winnipeg, this was one of those foreboding experiences. He has been foreboding so long that he is just foreboden now and he is ready to explode. He expected a bad bill-

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext: And got it.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext:
-and the bill is so good that he just cannot control himself; that is the whole thing. You know, the children of Israel we are told in the Bible many years ago that when they were in captivity in Egypt they had to make bricks without straw. Well, my hon. friend over there has been trying to make bricks without straw in connection with this bill and did not as well as is told us in the Bible.
Of course, anybody can quote from the Fowler commission report. You could probably take any sentence out of context, but he attempted at the beginning to say that this board of governors was something which was not recommended or contemplated by the Fowler commission. I read this excerpt from the report the other day but in view of the histrionic display just put on I think I should read it again. I am reading now from page 91 of the Fowler commission report:
The other public agency in the Canadian broadcasting field should be a board created and authorized to act for parliament, and responsible to parliament, for the direction and supervision of the Canadian broadcasting system. This board should have responsibility for all elements in Canadian broadcasting. It should not, we suggest, be part of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and its members should not, as in the present statute, comprise the corporation.

That is the statute under which we have been operating up to the present.
This board is not part of the C.B.C. and should not be referred to "as the board of governors of C.B.C.". We suggest that a new board, differently named, should be created by statute. The name we use in speaking of this agency is "the board of broadcast governors".
That contemplation, that vision, if you call it that, a term bandied around here a great deal lately, that recommendation of the Fowler commission has been accepted entirely by this government except for the fact that we have full-term personnel, three out of 15, instead of voluntary ones. I doubt whether there are any hon. members in this house who were prepared to go down the line of that phase of the Fowler commission report.
Reference was made by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson), or by someone else, to an article in the Journal by I. Norman Smith. No one would ever suggest that he was a critic of the C.B.C. or opposed to it. Mr. Norman Smith said that you could not accept that recommendation of the Fowler commission in so far as part-time officials were concerned. It is a great prospect. I do not think it would work. We put full-time men in there, three out of 15; we have 12 part-time men.
The absolute bankruptcy of any criticism of this bill on the part of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate is illustrated by what he did. He did not discuss the bill; he tried to try the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) on statements he made three or four years ago; he tried to put the Minister of Finance on trial. If that is the only criticism he could level against this bill, then it is a better bill than the other government brought in when they were sitting on the treasury benches. This bill is commended by both the radio league and officials of private broadcasting as well. It does not please everyone in every detail; it does not please me in every detail. No bill will ever please everyone; but it is a direct and honest effort made by this government to try to solve this problem which has been hanging over broadcasting for 15 years. It is not perfect; there will be mistakes in it. Undoubtedly, defects will be found, as I said the other night.
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, I think earlier in the day, referred to the history of the 1932 bill, or was it the Leader of the Opposition? He said that a royal commission had made studies and had held 45 meetings, and so on. I happened to be speaking to the gentleman who happened to be the vice-chairman of the board after it was appointed and he said that at their first

meeting, despite all that time-and time should be spent; time is always desirable- they found two sections of the act which were absolutely unworkable, and they had to improvise something in their place.
This afternoon the hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate referred to something he had said when he read the bill. I did not catch exactly what he said, but he said it reminded him of the Austria-Hungary empire; in other words, two parts, I presume, which could hardly function together, but that empire functioned for more or less a century. I would also remind him of the very distinguished member of the ancient Liberal party, one Goldwyn Smith, who said at one time that the federation of Canada was like a walnut; that it could not work, could not function. But Canada has functioned; Canada has worked; Canada is a nation. Anyone looking at the British commonwealth or at our system of government would say that it would not work. They would say that it was impossible, but it has worked. We know it has worked and we are proud of it. It is the same with this bill, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext: Impossible, but it will work.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext:
It will develop. Undoubtedly there will be faults in it. I am not suggesting for one moment that it is perfect legislation, or anything of that kind; but I do resent any suggestion that it is bringing the C.B.C. under government control or that it is attempting to make a political football out of the C.B.C., or anything of that kind.
We had a great deal of talk about those two men who are to be appointed at pleasure, but there is also a seven-year term, which is a fairly good indication that barring something absolutely inefficient, the seven years apply.
We have heard a great deal of talk about the absolute independence of this board of the C.B.C. I happened to look at the old act and I found that the general chairman of the board of governors of the C.B.C. was appointed for good behaviour, but it also says he shall be paid such annual salary as this nefarious creature, the governor in council, shall determine. He was appointed for a period of years. In other words, under the system of which we have heard so much boasting this afternoon the chairman of the board of governors of the C.B.C. was appointed at an annual salary that could be cut to $1 if the governor in council saw fit so to do. And yet they say we are trying to exercise some control. I am not suggesting that they did but I have heard it suggested. Certainly, no valid suggestion can be made against this government that it is attempting

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext:
The purpose of having the term of less than five years is to provide for the original, initial appointments so that you could stagger them and not have all the members retiring at the same time. A member could be appointed for two, three, four or five years. You will notice there is a provision that a member may be appointed for an additional term. It would then enable them to be appointed for a full term. This provides a continuity of officers. If all members had to be appointed for a period of five years you would have them all retiring on the one date. As the hon. member will appreciate the practice has grown up of staggering or rotating appointments and retirements.
As to the term of seven years, I suppose you could put your hand in a hat and draw out some other number. We wanted something to go on. We felt it should be more than five years. Men in the prime of life, or in middle life, coming here and giving up their occupations whatever they might be and accepting a position in Ottawa for a five-year term with one repeat and having to retire at age 70-they have to retire then anyway-might not be attracted by such a proposal. We thought it might not be too inviting and so it was decided to make a little longer term for the permanent officers with the thought and hope that it would perhaps assist in providing the type of personnel you might not get on the basis of a five-year term.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this particular provision which has been referred to by the hon. member for Port Arthur has caused some of us a good deal of worry. The minister will recall, of course, that the Fowler commission did recommend that there should be 15 part-time members for periods of five years. All members of the board under that commission recommendation would be part-time members. I am not quarrelling with the decision of the government to depart in principle from that recommendation, but I am worried about the way in which that departure has been made. If this bill becomes law we will have on this board of broadcast
Broadcasting
governors 12 part-time and three full-time members. They will also differ in their tenure of office, as has been pointed out. The fulltime members are appointed for seven years and the part-time members for five. There is another difference. The part-time members may serve only two consecutive terms, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Cartier, and then may not be re-appointed before a lapse of 12 months, while the three full-time members may serve as many terms as the government wishes. There is no requirement as I read the bill for a period of time to elapse before re-appointment.
What worries us in regard to this particular matter is the development inside this board of a-and I say this without offence-hierarchy of full-time members who will in fact be the dominating influence inside the board and who have been distinguished from the other members of the board in the ways which I have mentioned. This worry of ours is increased by the fact-and the minister mentioned that these three full-time members will serve on the executive committee which will be the day to day governing body for broadcasting in Canada, and the quorum of the executive committee is fixed at five.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext: Not the board of broadcast governors.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext: The executive committee.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext: Of the C.B.C.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext: Of the board of broadcast governors. If the minister will look up his bill I think he will find that is so.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext: Clause 9?

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext: It is at the top of page 4.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext: I beg your pardon; that refers to the quorum.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext:
The quorum of the executive committee is five, and since there are three full-time members of the board they could constitute a majority of the executive committee.
I can understand the chairman being appointed as a full-time member but I am worried about the appointment of three as full-time members. You might even make a case for the vice-chairman because he would have definite functions to perform as vice-chairman of the board, but this third member of which my hon. friend has spoken does seem to me to be in an anomalous position. He is one of this group of three who will have very great influence in directing this board but he seems to have no particular duties to perform. I suppose he is the third force among the permanent members of the board.

Broadcasting
We feel that if there is to be this distinction between part-time and full-time members-I can see the desirability of the distinction, perhaps, for the chairman,-it should not be brought any farther than is necessary. That is why we regret very much these other provisions which seem to emphasize and broaden the distinction between the full-time and part-time members. It does underline the danger which was mentioned this afternoon of this trio, the chairman, vice-chairman and the third member, becoming in fact a kind of hierarchy inside the board. I wonder whether the minister can reassure us on that point.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext:
I do not know just how much my assurances will reassure the Leader of the Opposition. I can understand that he would have some concern over that clause. It is an obvious one and one which I think quite justifies his raising the question which he has. He will notice to start with that the executive committee consists of seven. That was inserted deliberately so that the three- if there was to be any suspicion of them- would not have a majority on the executive committee. I misunderstood him a few moments ago because I thought he had referred to the executive committee. He is perfectly right in saying that the quorum can be five.
Now that is the situation. I think the only answer there, Mr. Chairman, is that if we select the people who should be selected for this executive committee-and I am assuming, although this does not necessarily follow; it is not limited in the legislation-they will be selected from this area, Montreal, Toronto, Ottawa; in other words, adjacent to Ottawa, and I would think that they should and usually would be in attendance at all meetings of the executive committee. That provision for seven was put in there deliberately so that there would be a majority of parttime men and women, if they came to the meeting.
The Leader of the Opposition says that these people will become a hierarchy. I hope not. I do not think they will if the right personnel are appointed. But I ask him, what is the alternative? If we had accepted in full the Fowler recommendations and had all part-time people on the board, I ask him, what would have been the result? I think it is a fair estimate-one can only assume things-that the secretariat, the permanent officials of the board, would have been the hierarchy and would have run the board and the part-time people coming in and going out would have been more or less, we will not say under the control but very strongly influenced by the permanent secretariat, the bureaucrats, to use perhaps an unfortunate phrase, of the board. That we want to avoid at all costs.

With all due respect to the secretariat, we think that the board should be run by Canadians who are selected for the purpose, rather than by officials who happen to be passed by the civil service commission and come to that board. As between the two, the secretariat which might even become the hierarchy and the three members of the board, I think the Leader of the Opposition will agree that perhaps this was the better alternative, although here again it depends on your personnel. It depends on experience, and there can be no guarantee of perfection whatever system is chosen.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext: Will the minister at some time clear up the point as to whether or not the existing members of the board of governors of the C.B.C. are eligible for appointment to the board of broadcast governors under this bill?

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext: I would have to get the advice of the Department of Justice on that. I will do that.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext: It is a fairly important point which should not be left hanging in the air. I appreciate the fact that the minister may not be able to answer it at the moment.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, in connection with the point I brought up before, it was subclause 6 I wanted the minister to look at rather than subclause 9. It seems to me that the second part of that subclause may rule out a member of the C.B.C. board of governors from becoming a member of the board of broadcast governors. I refer to the words "partner or otherwise". Take the case of a member of the staff of a university which owns a radio station. If you wanted to take a very narrow interpretation you could rule out such a person from becoming a member of the board of broadcast governors. I can think of several people who might be ideally suited and who would be ruled out on that ground. Could that not be made more specific?

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext: On that score I am quite sure that a university professor who was associated with a university which operated a broadcasting station would not come within the definition "engaged in the business of broadcasting or has any pecuniary or proprietary interest". Therefore I do not think you need to worry at all about the university professor. The question raised about the broadcast governors is exactly the same question as was raised by the hon. member for Ottawa West. I have my own opinion on it but it is not my opinion that will govern and, as I said, I will get a ruling from justice with respect to that point and give it either on the bill or on the estimates, depending on the progress we make with the bill.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext: Does the minister mean he has his own legal opinion on it or simply his own opinion as to the rightness of it?

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext: My own legal opinion but you are not interested in that.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext: There is one other question I want to raise. I take it it is quite clear that a member of the board of broadcast governors could not also be a director of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, or is that clear?

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext: I would hope so. If it is not, I can assure the hon. member that it will never happen as long as I am minister. I assume it is clear because there has to be an absolute divorce of the two.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext: I hope the minister will not misunderstand me if I tell him that in reading the bill before us I find some difficulty in understanding it in relation to his remarks. It seems to me that the bill is much broader than anything he indicated in his remarks, and that is what is bothering me.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, may I tell the minister at once that while not convinced I was impressed by his observation a few minutes ago on the composition of the board. He asked what we would have done. If I had had any authority in the matter I think I would have preferred to have a full-time chairman and the others all part-time. He suggests that if there were no full-time members or perhaps only one there would be a danger of the board falling into the hands of a secretariat of bureaucrats, as he called them without offence. But I suggest to him that when people are appointed for seven years and given a salary they are bureaucrats or will perhaps soon become bureaucrats in the best sense of the word.
I would also point out to the minister that in this clause all members of the board are appointed to hold office during good behaviour and that under subclause 7 no member of the board can be removed except on address of the Senate and House of Commons. That seems to me to be a very desirable provision in the legislation and is one reason why we are worried about the non-application of these two provisions-we will come to that later- to the board of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
While I am on my feet may I ask one further question about subclause 6 which has already been touched on by other hon. members. Under this provision a person who owns shares in a film company, perhaps a Canadian subsidiary of a United States film company, which happens to own a broadcasting station in Canada would, I take it, be disqualified from serving on this board. Would
Broadcasting
anybody who owned shares in a press association or chain of newspapers also be disqualified by ownership of shares in that press chain from sitting on this board if that press chain or corporation also ran a broadcasting station?

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext: I am not prepared to give a legal opinion on such a set of facts. As my hon. friend knows, every set of facts varies slightly one from another. All lawyers know that. I think a person would be very reckless to attempt to give a legal opinion today which would be of no avail anyway because if this matter were dealt with administratively it would have to be dealt with by justice and if it went further it would have to be dealt with by the courts. But I would suggest to the Leader of the Opposition that the words "directly or indirectly, as owner, shareholder, director, officer, partner or otherwise"-

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext: It is the "otherwise".

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext: -are very broad and will preclude many people from taking a position on the board. There can be no question about that. I do not want to try to give a legal definition of the area as to who is going to be excluded and who is going to be included.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext: But either the minister or some other minister or the Prime Minister is going to have to recommend certain names to the governor in council and the governor in council is going to have to appoint these people. Therefore it does seem to me that since parliament is being asked to make this enactment we should know precisely what this provision is supposed to mean. Would, for example, a shareholder in Canadian General Electric, which probably makes and sells parts of radio apparatus, be excluded or would somebody owning shares in Canadian Investment Fund, which might happen in turn to own some shares in Canadian General Electric, be thereby excluded? It seems to me that this is very vague and very far-reaching indeed and that perhaps it would be worth while to take another look at it for it might turn out that about the only people who will be eligible in the country will be farmers, fishermen and the unemployed.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext:
What about people engaged in the distribution of radio apparatus? Chain stores distribute radio apparatus. Would this apply to employees of chain stores? You can reduce this clause to an absurdity to illustrate the point I am seeking to make. It does not seem to be precisely or carefully worded. Perhaps the minister would give us what help he can. The clause causes me concern because taking certain illustrations one can see how easy it is to reduce it to an absurdity.

Broadcasting

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext: I think the minister as a lawyer is very sound and wise when he says that he will submit this discussion to the Department of Justice for a legal opinion. That is indeed very desirable. May I also suggest that when he does so he point out that it would be desirable that members of the present C.B.C. board should not be excluded from becoming members of the new board in order to retain the continuity he spoke about a few moments ago.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext:
May I bring clause 8 to the minister's attention? It seems to me to be so clear that I bring it to his attention in a particular way. The marginal note reads "duties of full-time members" and the clause reads as follows:
A full-time member shall devote the whole of his time to the performance of his duties under this part.
You might just as well have said that a full-time member shall work full-time. Is it necessary to include that clause? Does the minister not think that rather the duties of the members should be outlined and explained because there is not a word said about their duties other than that they are to work full time?

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext: The clause is put in there, of course, to make it plain that they shall not have any other occupation which is taking any of their time but shall devote their full time to the board. It can be expressed in various ways but the purpose is to make sure of that one salient fact. I think these men are going to be very busy at least for the first two or three years with meetings of the board, drafting regulations and dealing with licence applications, particularly if the government should determine as a matter of policy at some future time to restrict the present one channel outlets. I can see where there is going to be a great deal of business both for the full-time and the parttime members. You will notice somewhere else they are authorized to travel and hold meetings in other places. I certainly do not want them doing anything else, anyway.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext: Is there any definition other than that contained in this subclause 8 of the duties of the members of the board? I should like to say a word in connection with that.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext:
Clause 10, of course, relates to the general powers of the board. I have referred to that several times today. Then, clause 11 enumerates all the regulations

which the members of the board shall consider, debate, enact, promulgate and carry into effect.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext: I do not want to discuss these clauses before we come to them. Are the duties of the board going to be pretty much the same as they are now?

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext: So far as the C.B.C. board is concerned; that is the regulatory powers.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext: What I have in mind at the moment is an application for a radio station or a television broadcasting station. I presume the application will be made to the Minister of Transport in the usual course. It will be cleared by the Department of Transport in so far as the technical aspects are concerned, and then it will be forwarded to the board of broadcast governors who will consider this application and any others that may come before it at a public meeting?

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext: That is right.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext:
It has just occurred to me to wonder, since the hon. member for Laurier referred to this subsection providing that a full-time member shall be a full-time member, if I may abbreviate it, whether or not that would preclude these full-time members from being directors of any corporations. It does seem to me that is a point that ought to be made clear in this legislation one way or the other. Of course, some of the part-time members would be the kind of people who would be directors in other corporations. I would think there would be nothing improper in that. However, I wonder if any of them should be directors in advertising agencies. This might be just as serious a disqualification, perhaps more serious, than connection with a radio apparatus distribution firm such as Canadian General Electric or some other company that is rather remote from broadcasting.
In view of some of the debates we have had in previous sessions, it would be a good idea to determine whether or not these fulltime members can be directors of any company, especially any company from which they receive any remuneration and for which, I presume, they are expected to provide some service.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext: Does this subclause 8, in effect, prohibit any form of moonlighting?

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS- CONTINUANCE OF C.B.C.
speechtext: Absolutely.

Clause agreed to.
